(TI 2025-052/VII, 2025) and University of Twente et al., 'Engaging with cybercriminals: phases and influence strategies in ransomware negotiations', Computers in Human Behavior (2026), 41 authentic negotiation logs.

preconditions.statement: The shelter-jurisdiction check must pass. This is enforced in the build rather than in policy, which is why it survives enforcement pressure that voids every declared rule.
preconditions.basis: Mandiant (2021) documents the locale/keyboard-layout abort on CIS systems. It was the sole exclusion retained when a major brand publicly voided all others on 19-20 Dec 2023. Recorded Future Insikt Group, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), characterises the shelter as externally granted, selective, managed and revocable — which makes this precondition, uniquely among the four, something an intervention could in principle remove. Medium: the shelter relationship is inferred from arrest geography and prosecution patterns, not from any document either party has published.

preconditions.statement: Exfiltration must complete before encryption, because the retained copy is the only leverage that survives a successful restore.
preconditions.basis: Meurs et al. (TI 2025-052/VII, 2025) find backup status the dominant determinant of payment, which is what makes the exfiltrated copy load-bearing rather than supplementary. US government #StopRansomware victim guidance states payment does not guarantee deletion — the same fact from the other side, and the basis of the profile's no-verifiable-data-deletion item.

preconditions.statement: The victim must be revenue-estimable, because the demand is scaled to ability to pay rather than to the cost of the harm inflicted.
preconditions.basis: Meurs et al. (2025) document revenue-scaled dynamic pricing across 237 negotiation transcripts. Theoretical framing in Cartwright, Hernandez-Castro and Stepanova, 'To pay or not: game theoretic models of ransomware', Journal of Cybersecurity 5(1), 2019, on uniform pricing versus price discrimination versus bargaining. Chainalysis (2026) reports median payment up 368% to ~$59.5K alongside the record-low payment rate — the profile flags that this is at least partly a composition effect as smaller victims stop paying, not proof of harsher pricing.

preconditions.statement: A payment rail must exist that no sanctions designation has closed. This is an instrumental sensitivity to the victim's legal environment, not a legitimacy constraint, and it binds at settlement rather than at target selection.
preconditions.basis: OFAC designations of the brand and of hosting/laundering providers (Zservers Feb 2025; Aeza July 2025; Media Land Nov 2025) operate by converting payment into a legal act for the victim rather than by raising the actor's costs. Institute for Security and Technology, Ransomware Task Force, 'Combating Ransomware' (2021) and 'The RTF at 5 Years' (2026), frame the business model rather than the operators as the disruption target. The profile's legitimacyWeight basis insists this sensitivity be booked to cost and payment-channel variables, never to legitimacy.

afterAction.statement: There is no after-action review in an institutional sense. The institution dissolves, rebrands, and carries personnel, tooling and forum reputation into the successor; learning is embodied in code (locale guards, panel hardening, decentralised comms) and in market reputation rather than in doctrine. The practical consequence for a modeller is that a lesson learned by one brand is not reliably held by the next, and that disruption resets tradecraft far less than it resets branding.
afterAction.basis: Europol, IOCTA 2025 ('Steal, Deal and Repeat'), records 120+ active brands with affiliates and administrators operating across several of them simultaneously. Conti's wind-down on c. 19 May 2022 dispersed into successor brands rather than ending the operation (BleepingComputer, 19-21 May 2022; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, 'The rise and fall of the Conti ransomware group', 2023). Recorded Future, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), reports post-disruption tightening of affiliate vetting and a shift to decentralised communication platforms — the clearest observed instance of the ecosystem, rather than any single firm, updating. Medium: 'the ecosystem learns' is an aggregate claim assembled from brand-level observations, and no source demonstrates a within-brand review process.

declaredEnds.statement: Revenue, stated as the entire objective, with an explicit disclaimer of political ends.
declaredEnds.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021: 'We are apolitical, we do not participate in geopolitics, do not need to tie us with a defined government and look for our motives. Our goal is to make money, and not creating problems for society.' Contemporaneous reporting (Vice/Motherboard, 10 May 2021), used only as the actor's own declaratory text. Confidence is medium and not high for a reason the profile states plainly: this actor class lies in public postings, and the same statement's promise of target moderation was never observed to operate before the brand exited three days later.

declaredEnds.statement: Share of the licensee labour market, pursued explicitly and openly through publicity — the leak site is a recruitment instrument as much as a coercion instrument.
declaredEnds.basis: CISA/FBI AA23-165A, 14 June 2023, lists publicity-generating stunts among the means used to attract affiliates, including the frequently miscited $1M bounty offer, which the advisory categorises as a recruitment stunt rather than as evidence of anti-doxxing resolve. The leaked LockBit panel shows per-affiliate registration fees and accounting consistent with a programme sold to operators, not only run by them (Trellix, 2025). Affiliates were paid before the core, an inversion of normal practice that only makes sense as a labour-market reputation instrument (AA23-165A).

declaredEnds.statement: Continuity of the brand through law-enforcement disruption, declared as an objective in its own right and pursued at a loss.
declaredEnds.basis: LockBit posted an account of the Operation Cronos breach and its rebuild plan within five days of the 19 Feb 2024 seizure (BankInfoSecurity, Feb 2024; Trend Micro, 'Unveiling the Fallout: Operation Cronos' Impact on LockBit', Apr 2024), and the brand relaunched again as LockBit 5.0 in Sept 2025 with 15+ distinct victims identified in Q3 2025 (Check Point Research, Q3 2025). This is the one declared end the record shows being funded out of degraded revenue rather than out of profit, and it is the main tension with the profile's low ownCostTolerance.

selfImage.statement: Presents itself as a firm — a licensing business with a product, a support desk, a pricing policy and staff — rather than as a conspiracy or a political actor. Unusually for self-description, the internal record corroborates it: recovered material shows salaried employees, functional divisions and performance management rather than a loose crew.
selfImage.basis: The leaked Conti corpus shows salaried staff, an HR function, recruitment, and functional divisions; characterised by Check Point Research, 'Leaks of Conti Ransomware Group Paint Picture of a Surprisingly Normal Tech Start-Up... Sort Of' (Mar 2022), and analysed formally by Paternoster, Nazzari, Jofre and Uberti, Global Crime 26(2), 2025, 148-171, which finds a hierarchical, firm-like structure with discernible leadership and clear division of labour (n=168,740 messages; the first public tranche was ~60,000). Corroborating primary allegation: US DOJ, 20 Dec 2024, alleges a fixed ~$10,000/month salary for a core developer over 20 months — employment, not a share of proceeds. Medium: both windows are into brands that were compromised, and compromised brands may not be representative of the ~85 currently active.

threatModel.statement: Legal identification of its principals, and their presence in an extradition-cooperative jurisdiction. Infrastructure seizure is treated as a recoverable operating cost; identification is treated as the thing that cannot be undone.
threatModel.basis: Operation Cronos seized 34 servers, the affiliate panel, cryptocurrency addresses and 1,000+ decryption keys on 19 Feb 2024 (UK National Crime Agency, 20 Feb 2024) and the brand was operating again within five days (Trend Micro, Apr 2024). The May 2024 NCA/OFAC/AFP identification and designation of the brand's lead degraded it further, yet it relaunched in Sept 2025 (Check Point, Q3 2025). Which of the two did the greater damage is contested rather than settled: Analyst1, 'LockBit Takedown and Operation Cronos' (2024) and 'Ransomware Diaries Volume 5' (2024-25), attributes the licensee exodus and the collapse in affiliate access pricing to the seizure operation itself. The profile treats this as its least defensible parameter for exactly this reason.

threatModel.statement: Insiders and infiltrators — the disclosure risk it can neither price nor insure against, and the reason the vetting gate exists at all.
threatModel.basis: The Feb-Mar 2022 leak of Conti's internal chats by an apparent insider objecting to the group's pro-Kremlin statement (TechCrunch, 28 Feb 2022; The Record, Mar 2022). The 7 May 2025 defacement of a LockBit panel and publication of its database dump by an unidentified actor (Trellix, 2025). Recorded Future, Dark Covenant 3.0 (2025), reports eroding trust inside the underground, with affiliates complaining of scams, impersonation and selective enforcement. Medium: the 2025 panel hacker's motive and identity remain unknown, so it evidences the exposure rather than the source of it.

threatModel.statement: Revocation of the shelter it operates under — a conditional, externally granted permission rather than a possession, and the only threat on this list the actor cannot mitigate through tradecraft.
threatModel.basis: Recorded Future Insikt Group, Dark Covenant 3.0: Controlled Impunity and Russia's Cybercriminals (events through Sept 2025), describes a shift from passive tolerance to selective, managed and revocable enforcement. Confidence is capped at low-to-medium: the relationship is inferred from arrest and prosecution patterns by a commercial intelligence vendor, no primary document from either side exists, and the profile's uncertainty section names this as the single most behaviourally consequential thing its schema cannot currently represent.

threatModel.statement: Victims who can restore without paying, together with the professionalised incident-response, negotiation and insurance apparatus around them — a commercial threat to the revenue model rather than a threat to the operators.
threatModel.basis: Meurs et al. (2025) find backup status the dominant determinant of payment across 481 incidents. Chainalysis (2026) reports payments falling to $820M in 2025, down 8% year on year and 35% from 2023's $1.25B, with the payment rate at ~28% against a 50% rise in claimed attacks — the actor is attacking more and collecting less. Sophos (2025) finds 71% of ransom reductions were obtained through negotiation, i.e. by a professionalised counterparty.

adversaryModel.statement: Models the victim as a rational payer whose decision turns on restorability and disclosure exposure rather than on principle, and expects to negotiate — a high opening demand followed by a large discount is the designed path, not a failure. It models law enforcement as able to take infrastructure and money but not persons inside the shelter, which is why it treats a takedown as an operating cost and does not retaliate against it. Both models are partly wrong, and the same way: it consistently underestimates the probability that a victim it selected commercially triggers a state-level response.
adversaryModel.basis: Negotiation expectations: Sophos, State of Ransomware 2025 (payers averaged 85% of the initial demand; 53% paid below ask, 29% at ask, 18% above; 71% of reductions via negotiation) and Meurs et al. (2025) on the six-stage structure. Law-enforcement model: the observed response to Operation Cronos was reconstitution, not reprisal (NCA, Feb 2024; Trend Micro, Apr 2024). The overconfidence finding rests on two episodes — Colonial Pipeline (May 2021) and Kaseya (July 2021) — which is thin evidence for a general claim, and is the reason the profile encodes escalationControlBelief as a belief the record shows to be overconfident rather than as demonstrated capability.

declaredIdeology.statement: The only programmatic text this actor class issues about itself is an affiliate rules-of-engagement posting: an explicitly apolitical profit doctrine plus a target-exclusion list. Both limbs are unreliable in specific, checkable ways. The exclusions are drafted to preserve the revenue-bearing limb — one brand's published rule prohibited encrypting medical institutions 'where attacks could lead to death' while expressly permitting theft of their data — and another brand voided every exclusion but the shelter jurisdiction within hours of a law-enforcement seizure. There is no political, territorial or normative programme, and the profile's strongest negative finding is that this actor has no ideological redline to protect.
declaredIdeology.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021 (apolitical, profit-motivated, announcing target moderation). LockBit's published affiliate rules prohibiting encryption of medical institutions while permitting data theft from them, reported in the coverage of its 31 Dec 2022 SickKids reversal (BleepingComputer, 1 Jan 2023; CSO Online, Jan 2023). ALPHV/BlackCat's 19-20 Dec 2023 rules posting: 'we are introducing new rules, or rather removing ALL the rules except one, you can not touch the CIS, you can now block hospitals, nuclear power plants, anything and anywhere' (contemporaneous reporting, BleepingComputer; Barracuda Networks blog, Mar 2024); the underlying disruption is documented in CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-353A, '#StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat' (Dec 2023 update). Confidence is low and should stay low: these are self-published postings by an actor class that lies in public, and the profile's declaredVsObserved section records that observed targeting contradicts every exclusion in them.

history.episode: Three US federal agencies issued an unprecedented joint advisory warning of an 'increased and imminent cybercrime threat' to US hospitals, naming Ryuk and Conti, while the operators were mid-campaign against the healthcare sector during the COVID-19 pandemic.
history.choice: Acted, and kept acting. The operators pressed a campaign against hospitals at the point of maximum leverage and maximum political heat, and did not stand down when three federal agencies named them in public.
history.lesson: Acted, and absorbed public attribution without changing behaviour. The clearest observed evidence that harm to noncombatants is not a constraint on this institution but a source of coercive leverage, and that being named by a government is not by itself a cost it prices. It is the observed-conduct anchor for counterpartHarmRestraint at 0.15, against declared exclusions that would have implied roughly 0.45.
history.basis: CISA, FBI and HHS, Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA20-302A, 'Ransomware Activity Targeting the Healthcare and Public Health Sector', 28 Oct 2020, updated 29 Oct 2020 to add Conti, TrickBot and BazarLoader. Consequence anchor rather than preference measure: McGlave, Neprash and Nikpay, 'Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients', American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 18(1), 2026, 256-81, find in-hospital mortality rises 34-38% for patients already admitted when an attack begins. Medium rather than high because the continuation is the aggregate of many licensees' separate choices, not a recorded institutional decision to persist.

history.episode: Eleven days after the Colonial Pipeline attack triggered a US fuel-supply emergency and direct presidential comment, DarkSide announced it had lost its infrastructure and funds and wound the brand down. Three days earlier it had posted that it was apolitical, that its goal was 'to make money, and not creating problems for society', and that from that day it would check each company its partners wanted to encrypt.
history.choice: Withdrew. It abandoned the brand rather than carry state-level attention, and issued a target-vetting policy only after the incident that prompted it.
history.lesson: Held nothing and dissolved. The institution absorbs almost no enforcement cost: it exits and re-forms rather than paying to keep a brand alive. It also fixes the ceiling on escalation control — a licensee's ordinary commercial target selection produced a national-emergency response the core neither predicted nor wanted, which is why escalationControlBelief encodes a belief rather than a demonstrated capability. The apolitical statement is a legitimacy claim addressed to the labour market and the shelter, not a constraint that operated before the attack.
history.basis: DarkSide's 'About the latest news' posting, c. 10 May 2021, and its 13 May 2021 shutdown announcement, both as reported contemporaneously (Vice/Motherboard, 10 May 2021; Axios, 14 May 2021) — journalism, used only for the actor's own declaratory text. Mandiant, 'Shining a Light on DARKSIDE Ransomware Operations' (2021), for the affiliate rules of engagement and the CIS locale check. The profile's declaredVsObserved section records the vetting promise as a post-hoc announcement of future vetting followed by brand exit, not as evidence of pre-emptive target avoidance, and this episode should not be cited as restraint.

history.episode: Conti declared 'full support of the Russian government' on 25 Feb 2022 and threatened critical-infrastructure reprisals against anyone attacking Russia; an apparent insider objecting to that statement leaked the group's internal chats within days; the operation wound down around 19 May 2022 and dispersed into successor brands.
history.choice: Acted politically once, then absorbed a catastrophic internal disclosure and dissolved rather than defend the brand.
history.lesson: Acted, then dissolved. The single episode in the record where this actor class took a political side, and it was punished from inside its own organisation — which is why the profile carries no ideological redline and why any values-based hard constraint on this actor would be an artifact. The wind-down was multi-causal (a costly campaign against one government, sanctions converting payment into a legal act, and the leak), so it is not clean evidence that the disclosure alone ended the brand. The same corpus is simultaneously the strongest evidence that the core is a hierarchical firm rather than a loose network, and is the principal counter-evidence against a low decisionCentralization value.
history.basis: Conti's 25 Feb 2022 posting and the ContiLeaks disclosure beginning 27-28 Feb 2022 (TechCrunch, 28 Feb 2022; The Record, Mar 2022; Check Point Research, Mar 2022, on the first tranche of ~60,094 messages). Wind-down reported 19-21 May 2022 (BleepingComputer; The Hacker News). Structure findings on the full corpus (n=168,740): Paternoster, Nazzari, Jofre and Uberti, Global Crime 26(2), 2025, 148-171, doi:10.1080/17440572.2025.2473350, and a companion 2025 Global Crime study on organisational units and communication patterns, doi:10.1080/17440572.2025.2534387 (paywalled; abstract only).

history.episode: Thirteen days after a licensee encrypted the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, the LockBit core publicly apologised on its leak site, published a free decryptor, and stated that the licensee had violated its rules and had been expelled from the affiliate programme. The hospital did not pay and did not use the decryptor.
history.choice: Refused, retroactively. It forfeited the revenue on a live extortion and expelled the licensee — the only sanction the core actually holds.
history.lesson: Held — but only after the fact, and only on the limb of the rule that does not bear revenue. The published rule prohibited encrypting medical institutions where the attack could cause death while expressly permitting theft of their data, so the enforcement action protected standing in the licensee labour market at close to the minimum commercial cost. It is genuine restraint and it is narrow: the same brand appears in a government advisory as a healthcare attacker six months later. The episode also locates authority precisely — the core can expel a licensee after the fact and cannot prevent the attack — which is the split the profile's decisionCentralization note describes.
history.basis: LockBit's leak-site posting of 31 Dec 2022 and the free decryptor, reported contemporaneously (BleepingComputer, 1 Jan 2023; CSO Online, Jan 2023; Healthcare IT News, Jan 2023; Infosecurity Magazine). The hospital's confirmation that it neither paid nor used the decryptor (CBC News, Jan 2023). The encrypt-versus-exfiltrate carve-out in the published rules appears in the same coverage. Continued sector targeting: CISA/FBI AA23-165A, 14 June 2023, lists healthcare among sectors attacked by LockBit affiliates. Medium: the apology is the actor's own declaratory text and the motive attributed to it is inferred, not documented.

history.episode: Cl0p claimed mass exploitation of a MOVEit Transfer zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) it had been testing since at least July 2021, launched over the US Memorial Day weekend beginning 27 May 2023; days later it posted that government, city and police victims need 'not worry, we erased all your data'.
history.choice: Acted at scale on a capability held unspent for roughly two years, and simultaneously declined to extort one class of victim.
history.lesson: Held, then acted. Contradicts a purely short-horizon reading of this actor: the capability was held for about two years and released only once the tooling supported mass simultaneous collection, which is why timeHorizon is encoded at 0.3 rather than at the near-zero the 22-second handoff figure would suggest. The declared carve-out for government and police victims is not restraint about harm — it is avoidance of the single response class the actor cannot absorb, and it was never verified; federal agencies were confirmed among the compromised. Brand attribution was sought loudly at the same moment legal exposure was minimised, which is exactly the split construct attributionAversion encodes.
history.basis: Kroll, 'Clop Ransomware: MOVEit Transfer Vulnerability CVE-2023-34362' (June 2023), dates manual exploitation testing to July 2021, automated multi-organisation probing from April 2022, scaled activity from 15 May 2023, and mass exploitation from 27 May 2023. CISA and FBI, Advisory AA23-158A, '#StopRansomware: CL0P Ransomware Gang Exploits CVE-2023-34362 MOVEit Vulnerability', 7 June 2023. The 'we erased all your data' text is the actor's own leak-site posting, reported contemporaneously (The Record, 6 June 2023). Medium: the deletion claim is unverifiable and should be read as declaratory, and the two-year hold is Kroll's forensic inference from command similarity rather than a recovered decision record.

history.episode: ALPHV/BlackCat filed a whistleblower complaint with the US Securities and Exchange Commission against its own victim, MeridianLink, for failing to disclose the breach, published a screenshot of the complaint under the headline 'MeridianLink fails to file with the SEC ...so we do it for them', and attached a 24-hour deadline.
history.choice: Escalated into the victim's regulatory environment rather than into further technical harm.
history.lesson: Escalated, through law rather than through damage. This is what the profile means by zero normative legitimacy weight combined with high instrumental sensitivity to the victim's legal environment: the actor invokes a regulator whose jurisdiction it is itself a fugitive from, because the victim's disclosure exposure is a cheaper lever than more encryption. It also shows the escalation-control belief is overconfident in a checkable way — the disclosure rule the complaint relied on had not yet reached its compliance date, so the lever the actor believed it was pulling did not exist.
history.basis: ALPHV's leak-site posting and published complaint screenshot, reported 15-16 Nov 2023 (BleepingComputer; SecurityWeek; The Record, which also reported MeridianLink's confirmation of the incident). The SEC's cybersecurity disclosure requirement (Form 8-K Item 1.05, adopted July 2023) had a compliance date of 18 Dec 2023 for most registrants and later for smaller reporting companies — after the complaint was filed. Medium: the event and the timing gap are well documented; the inference about what the actor believed is exactly that, an inference.

history.episode: Hours after an FBI-led operation seized its leak site and distributed decryption keys, ALPHV/BlackCat re-established infrastructure and posted new rules: 'we are introducing new rules, or rather removing ALL the rules except one, you can not touch the CIS, you can now block hospitals, nuclear power plants, anything and anywhere'.
history.choice: Escalated under a loss frame — voided every declared targeting limit except the shelter jurisdiction and widened what its licensees were permitted to attack.
history.lesson: Escalated. Under enforcement pressure the institution accepts risk it otherwise avoids, and the risk it spends is other people's safety rather than its own exposure — the one rule retained was the one protecting its principals. It also identifies where the binding constraint actually sits: the asset worth voiding every remaining rule for is the licensee labour base, because the core cannot generate victims without it, which is the behavioural content of proxyPreference at 0.85. The episode is the primary evidence for lossFrameRiskAcceptance at 0.65.
history.basis: ALPHV's 19-20 Dec 2023 rules posting, reported contemporaneously (BleepingComputer; Barracuda Networks blog, Mar 2024) — declaratory text from an actor class that lies in public, therefore corroborative only. The underlying disruption is documented in CISA/FBI Advisory AA23-353A, '#StopRansomware: ALPHV Blackcat' (Dec 2023 update), and in the US DOJ/FBI announcement of 19 Dec 2023. The consequence is recorded in the same advisory's 27 Feb 2024 update, which states that since mid-December 2023, of the nearly 70 leaked victims, healthcare was the most commonly victimised sector, 'likely in response to the ALPHV Blackcat administrator's post encouraging its affiliates to target hospitals after operational action against the group and its infrastructure in early December 2023'.

history.episode: After a licensee's attack on Change Healthcare produced an apparent ~$22M payment, the ALPHV core took the entire payment, posted a fake law-enforcement seizure banner on its own site, and exited — defrauding the licensee, which still held the exfiltrated data and said so publicly.
history.choice: Defected against its own surrogate, taking a one-time cash-out over the continuing enterprise.
history.lesson: Acted, at the expense of the enterprise. Bounds the time horizon from above: offered a large enough single payment, the core will liquidate its own brand and its own labour relationships rather than compound them, which is the main evidence against reading timeHorizon up toward the multi-year brand persistence the same actor otherwise displays. It locates the payment rail firmly with the core — the licensee could not collect around it. And it is the concrete demonstration that a settlement cannot bind whoever physically holds the data, which is why the no-verifiable-data-deletion item is an inability to commit rather than a refusal.
history.basis: B. Krebs, 'BlackCat Ransomware Group Implodes After Apparent $22M Ransom Payment by Change Healthcare', Krebs on Security, 5 Mar 2024, reporting the affiliate's own account posted to a Russian-language crime forum; corroborated by contemporaneous coverage (S-RM, Cyber Intelligence Briefing, 12 Mar 2024; HIPAA Journal, Mar 2024). Medium and not higher: the affiliate's account is self-interested, and the payment was not confirmed by the victim at the time of the episode.

history.episode: Operation Cronos seized 34 servers, the affiliate panel, cryptocurrency addresses and over 1,000 decryption keys from LockBit. The brand re-established a leak site within five days, continued operating through the May 2024 identification and designation of its lead, and relaunched again as LockBit 5.0 in September 2025.
history.choice: Absorbed the loss and rebuilt. It did not retaliate against law enforcement and it did not alter its jurisdiction of residence.
history.lesson: Absorbed cost — the standing exception to this actor's otherwise low cost tolerance, and the episode that marks where the real commitment sits. Brand and infrastructure are replaceable and were replaced; what was never traded at any price was the principals' legal identity or their presence in a non-extraditing jurisdiction, which is the principal-liberty-preservation redline. Against a state adversary it shows no reciprocity whatsoever: no reprisal, only reconstitution, which is why the profile carries no compels_response redline and treats any modelled tit-for-tat here as an artifact. The contested part matters: Analyst1 attributes the licensee exodus and the collapse in affiliate access pricing (~$10,000 to ~$700) to the seizure itself rather than to the later public identification, so 'naming the lead was decisive' is not established.
history.basis: UK National Crime Agency, 'The NCA announces the disruption of LockBit with Operation Cronos', 20 Feb 2024. Trend Micro, 'Unveiling the Fallout: Operation Cronos' Impact on LockBit Following Landmark Disruption', Apr 2024; five-day relaunch reported contemporaneously (BankInfoSecurity; Dark Reading, Feb 2024). May 2024 NCA/OFAC/AFP designation of the brand's lead. Relaunch and Q3 2025 victim count: Check Point Research, 'LockBit 5.0: Ransomware Gang Returns in Force' (2025). Contested causal attribution: Analyst1, 'LockBit Takedown & Operation Cronos: A Long-Awaited PsyOps Against Ransomware' (2024) and 'Ransomware Diaries Volume 5' (2024-25).

weakestClaim.finding: the only stage set to low confidence. The core-set price floor and delegated discount authority are inferred from the observed discount distribution (Sophos 2025: 53% of payers paid below ask, payers averaged 85%) and from the chat controls visible in the May 2025 LockBit panel dump; no recovered pricing-policy document states a floor, so a modeller should treat that gate as plausible mechanism rather than established fact. Close second: worldview.threatModel[2] (revocation of the shelter jurisdiction, also low) — behaviourally the most consequential claim in the dossier and it rests on a single commercial-vendor assessment (Recorded Future, Dark Covenant 3.0, 2025) inferred from arrest and prosecution patterns, with no primary document from either party. worldview.declaredIdeology is marked low by construction: it cites only self-published affiliate rules-of-engagement postings from an actor class whose declared exclusions the profile's own declaredVsObserved section shows to be contradicted by observed targeting.

profiles.label: Ideologically-motivated violent non-state actor
profiles.summary: This archetype decides as a clandestine, mobilization-dependent organization whose choices are governed by movement survival and constituency signalling rather than by international-legal standing: it accepts very high costs among operational personnel, weights international legitimacy near zero, and treats harm to noncombatants as instrumentally available rather than as a bound. Command structure is genuinely bimodal — either a hierarchical leadership council with few internal vetoes, or a leaderless/self-directed pattern with almost no central authority — so a midpoint value describes no real organization and scenarios should sample the two modes separately. Leadership believes it can steer an escalation ladder more than it actually can, delegating to affiliates and remotely guided sympathizers for reach and survivability rather than for deniability, which is why attack-level attribution runs low while movement-level propaganda visibility runs high. Its declared goals are generational while its operational tempo is impatient, and only its constitutive claim, its armed character, and the continuity of its command core sit outside cost-benefit.

ownCostTolerance.basis: ASYMMETRIC, not uniform: high tolerance for losses among operational personnel, low tolerance for losses among cadre/command (see redline on leadership survivability). Hafez, Manufacturing Human Bombs (USIP 2006): martyrdom is organizationally produced and rationed, implying leadership manages operative expenditure as a resource rather than treating it as unbounded. Downgraded from 'high' because the devoted-actor evidence is a LEVEL-OF-ANALYSIS MISMATCH: Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (PNAS 2007) measures attitudes of conflict POPULATIONS (settlers, refugees, students), not organizational leadership decisions, and Atran, Sheikh & Gomez (PNAS 111(50), 2014) is a two-page COMMENTARY, not an empirical study. A single scalar cannot express the cadre/operative split.

counterpartHarmRestraint.basis: Value widened and confidence cut. The prior basis was partly CIRCULAR: defining the archetype by noncombatant targeting and then citing that definition as evidence of low restraint is not evidence. Kydd & Walter (Intl Security 31(1), 2006) supplies the strategic logic, not a restraint measurement. Substantial cross-group and within-group VARIATION is documented in Stanton, Violence and Restraint in Civil War (Cambridge 2016) and Jo, Compliant Rebels (Cambridge 2015); active moral and organizational brakes in Busher, Holbrook & Macklin (CREST 2019). Polo & Welsh (IO 78(3), 2024 - note published corrigendum, IO 78(3):625) find extreme violent competition yields restraint. Treat as high-variance across cases, not a stable archetype trait; scenarios should sample rather than fix.

attributionAversion.basis: Abrahms & Conrad (Security Studies 26(2), 2017): only ~1 in 7 attacks claimed; leaders often actively deny involvement; anonymity chosen where backlash risk is high. Retained at 0.25 but see the explicit reconciliation note under signalingPreference - movement-level propaganda visibility and attack-level attribution are DIFFERENT channels and must not be collapsed.

proxyPreference.basis: Franchise/affiliate structures plus remote direction of sympathizers (Hughes & Meleagrou-Hitchens, CTC Sentinel 10(3), 2017); intermediated financing. SCHEMA CAVEAT: this value encodes REACH and mobilization, NOT deniability-seeking - the two motives are conflated by the parameter name. A consumer reading 0.6 as deniability preference will mis-predict; deniability is captured by attributionAversion, which is low.

escalationControlBelief.basis: RAISED, because the prior value conflated BELIEF with CAPABILITY. Shapiro, The Terrorist's Dilemma (Princeton 2013) and Watkins (CTC Sentinel 2016) are evidence about ACTUAL control (principal-agent slippage, bottom-up momentum leadership 'cannot fully control'), not about what leadership BELIEVES. Provocation strategy (Kydd & Walter 2006) presupposes leaders believe they can steer the escalation ladder even where they demonstrably cannot. DECLARED/BELIEVED control therefore exceeds DEMONSTRATED control; a parameter named 'belief' must carry the former. Confidence low: no source directly measures leadership beliefs about controllability.

timeHorizon.basis: CORRECTED SOURCE READING. Phillips (T&PV 31(6), 2019, 1255-1265) was previously cited backwards: his paper DEBUNKS the high-mortality conventional wisdom, concluding terrorist organizations are MORE durable than assumed (~50% mean first-year failure across eight datasets, range 25-74%). Cronin, How Terrorism Ends (Princeton 2009): median lifespan ~5-10 years, which supports a LONGER horizon than the prior 0.4. Additional unaddressed problem: SURVIVORSHIP - unconditional first-year mortality is the wrong base rate for scenarios modeling groups that have already survived year one. Declared generational struggle vs observed tempo pressure from visibility-funded recruitment keeps this below midpoint, but confidence is low.

decisionCentralization.basis: GENUINELY BIMODAL - and a midpoint is therefore the value the actor is LEAST likely to occupy. Hierarchical leader/council authority with few internal vetoes (~0.8) versus leaderless-resistance and self-directed cells (~0.25) (Shapiro 2013 on covert delegation; RAND RBA1841-1, 2022; GNET 2022; ODNI ATA 2025 on decentralized affiliate structures). MODELING DIRECTIVE: scenarios should sample the two modes, not this mean, which describes no real organization. Term note: use neutral 'leadership council' - the prior basis used 'shura', an Arabic/Islamic governance term, as the generic descriptor for the whole archetype.

lossFrameRiskAcceptance.basis: Watkins (CTC Sentinel 2016): territorial loss correlated with escalated external attacks in the Islamic State case. CONFIDENCE CUT because this is substantially a SINGLE-CASE inference generalized to an archetype, and it is directly contested by Polo & Welsh (IO 78(3), 2024, 290 organizations 1970-2018), where competitive/existential pressure produces RESTRAINT rather than escalation. Two credible bodies of evidence point opposite directions; the disagreement is unresolved in the open literature and the value should be treated as a wide band (0.5-0.85), not a point.

legitimacyWeight.basis: SCOPE-LIMITED: this scalar covers INTERNATIONAL-LEGAL/UN legitimacy only, which is not this archetype's audience (Jo, Compliant Rebels 2015: IHL compliance sits with recognition-seeking rebels). CRITICAL SCHEMA GAP: the redline set states that SYMBOLIC concessions - adversary acknowledgment of the claim's validity, apology - do move devoted actors where material inducements do not (Ginges/Atran line). Adversary-recognition legitimacy and constituency legitimacy are therefore HIGH-salience channels that this near-floor scalar cannot express, and a simulation reading 0.12-0.15 as global legitimacy indifference will ignore the one concession class the literature says works. Two-significant-figure precision (0.12) was unearned; this is an ordinal near-floor judgment, not a measurement.

signalingPreference.basis: LOWERED AND DOWNGRADED to resolve a direct INTERNAL CONTRADICTION with this profile's own attributionAversion basis: 0.9/high cannot coexist with Abrahms & Conrad's finding that ~6 of 7 attacks go unclaimed and leaders often deny involvement. Reconciliation: signaling operates strongly at MOVEMENT/propaganda level (Kydd & Walter 2006 costly signaling to enemy and constituency; ODNI ATA 2025 on media aimed at inspiring self-directed supporters) but weakly at ATTACK-ATTRIBUTION level. Jenkins (RAND P-5261, 1974) 'terrorism is theater' / 'a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead' is retained as foundational but flagged as SUBSTANTIALLY REVISED by the post-1990s mass-casualty literature; a 1974 paper should not anchor a high-confidence 2026 rating.

reciprocityProportion.basis: SEMANTICS DISAMBIGUATED: this value encodes INTENDED response magnitude, not realized behavior. The prior basis was self-contradictory - 'deliberately outsized' describes DISproportion and cannot justify a proportionality parameter, while 'capability-capped, below intent' describes a different quantity. Retaliation is framed expressively and provocation seeks a disproportionate STATE response (Kydd & Walter 2006). Realized reciprocity is capability-capped and materially lower. Confidence low until the schema separates intended from realized magnitude.

redlines.statement: The organization's constitutive claim - the territory, status, or identity-defining grievance that supplies its reason to exist - is not exchangeable for material compensation. Economic or material inducements offered in return for relinquishing that claim are refused within the scenario horizon, and raising the offer does not raise the probability of acceptance; the measured effect runs the wrong way.
redlines.basis: Ginges, Atran & Medin, 'Sacred bounds on rational resolution of violent political conflict,' PNAS 104(18) 2007, 7357-7360 (material-inducement backfire on values held as non-fungible); replicated in Atran, 'The Devoted Actor,' Current Anthropology 57(S13) 2016. Deliberately NOT resting on the PNAS 2014 item the earlier draft cited: that is Atran, Sheikh & Gomez, PNAS 111(50):17702-17703, a two-page commentary rather than an empirical study, with the author list and Ginges's authorship stated incorrectly in the source profile. The 2007 experimental result is load-bearing on its own.

redlines.statement: The organization retains its armed apparatus and does not renounce the in-principle legitimacy of armed action. Ceasefires, thresholds and target restrictions are treated as tactical, reversible and internally contested; disarmament is treated as dissolution rather than as a bargaining chip, because the group has no non-violent institutional form to fall back into.
redlines.basis: Busher, Holbrook & Macklin, 'The internal brakes on violent escalation: a typology' (CREST 2019 full report; Behavioral Sciences of Terrorism and Political Aggression 2019): documented restraint logics bear on the forms and thresholds of violence, not on the in-principle legitimacy of armed action. Shapiro, The Terrorist's Dilemma (Princeton 2013) on the covert organization's dependence on its operational core. Weaker on the disarmament half: the only war-to-peace-transition support is the 'Navigating Uncertainty' Perspectives on Politics 2024 reflection essay, which is an essay rather than a systematic study, and decade-plus counter-cases exist (Provisional IRA decommissioning), so this holds only inside a months-to-few-years horizon.

redlines.statement: Continuity of the command cadre and of the organization itself is treated as a floor rather than a tradeable cost, even while losses among operational personnel are accepted at very high rates. Courses of action that expend the leadership council or the organizational core are refused irrespective of the payoff attached to them.
redlines.basis: Jones & Libicki, How Terrorist Groups End, RAND MG-741-1 (2008): policing and intelligence pressure on key members is the most common cause of group death (~40%), so command continuity is managed as a survival condition. Hafez, Manufacturing Human Bombs (USIP 2006): operative expenditure is organizationally produced and rationed, i.e. leadership treats personnel as a managed resource rather than an unbounded one. Coded low-confidence because this may be more honestly represented as the asymmetry inside ownCostTolerance (high for operatives, low for cadre) than as a genuine non-negotiable.

profiles.uncertainty:
## READ FIRST — calibration limit: this is not a validated general model of ideological violence

**The archetype label claims generality that its evidence base does not support.** Nearly every value here is calibrated on one religiously-framed movement family (Salafi-jihadist cases): territorial-loss escalation drives `lossFrameRiskAcceptance`; remote direction of sympathizers drives `proxyPreference`; organizationally produced suicide operations drive `ownCostTolerance`; and the devoted-actor experiments behind the first redline draw their samples from a single conflict theater. The two sources on racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism (RAND RBA1841-1, 2022; GNET 2022) appear **only** to destabilise `decisionCentralization` — they move no value. No ethno-nationalist, left-revolutionary, or single-issue case informs any parameter.

**Consequence for use:** treat this as a profile of one movement family wearing a generic label. It should not be run as a generic "ideological violence" actor, and any finding produced with it should be reported as scoped to that family until the sourcing is rebalanced or the archetype is renamed to match its evidence.

**Vocabulary correction applied.** The prior draft used a faith-specific governance term as the generic structural descriptor for the whole archetype. It is replaced throughout with "leadership council"; no analytic content changes. Framing devices are named as the group's own (a constitutive or identity-defining claim), never as a property of a population, and operative expenditure is described as organizationally produced rather than as a cultural disposition.

## Why all three constraints are null

None of the three commitments is a bound on `civilianHarmShare`, `legitimacyCost`, `visibility`, or `attributability`. They are bounds on *what may be traded away* (the constitutive claim, the armed apparatus) and on *whose losses may be spent* (the command core). The schema has no own-cost or bargaining-object attribute, so honest coding leaves `constraint: null` rather than inventing a numeric ceiling. Two mappings were considered and rejected: (a) binding the cadre floor to `attributability` — attributability measures whether an act is traced to whoever ordered it, not whether command is exposed to attrition, and conflating them would silently duplicate `attributionAversion`; (b) binding anything to `civilianHarmShare` — the internal-brakes literature is explicit that restraint on forms and thresholds is tactical, reversible and contested, i.e. a weight, not a refusal. **As coded, these redlines will not change the engine's move set.** If the engine needs them to bite, the schema needs a "bargaining object off the table" predicate; that is a schema gap, not an actor finding.

## Commitments deliberately NOT coded as redlines

- **Refusal to recognise the adversary's legitimacy.** The cited experimental line actually shows the opposite of a refusal: *symbolic* concessions (acknowledgment that the claim is valid, an apology) move this actor where material sweeteners do not. That is responsiveness, not a redline. It does expose a real modelling error: at `legitimacyWeight` 0.15 the simulation will discount the only concession class the literature says works. Legitimacy here is not weightless, it is differently weighted — international-legal standing near zero, adversary acknowledgment of the claim non-trivial. This is the most consequential downstream distortion in the profile.
- **Obligation to imprisoned or captured members.** Case-supported only; no systematic cross-group study. A soft, evidence-thin regularity is not a redline.
- **All three coded redlines are horizon-bounded.** They hold across months to a few years. Over decade-plus horizons and after leadership generational change several have historically become tradeable (Provisional IRA decommissioning is the standing counter-case). Do not code them as permanent.

## Least defensible parameters, in order

1. `decisionCentralization` 0.60 (low) — a genuinely bimodal distribution reported as its mean. Hierarchical clandestine organizations sit ~0.75-0.85; leaderless/self-directed movements ~0.10-0.25. The midpoint is the value the actor is *least* likely to occupy. Split into two actor variants rather than averaging.
2. `rationalityPrecision` 4 (low) — the basis states a range of 3-6 and then reports a bare point. Invented precision on top of an unresolved thirty-year dispute between the strategic-signalling school and the organizational-incentive critique; carry the band, not the point.
3. `counterpartHarmRestraint` 0.20 (low) — the earlier justification was circular (defining the archetype by noncombatant targeting, then citing that definition as evidence of low restraint). Cross-group and within-group variation is large; treat as high-variance, and do not read it as an upper bound on lethality intent.
4. `lossFrameRiskAcceptance` 0.75 (low) — substantially a single-case inference generalised to an archetype, and directly contested by a 290-organization study the profile itself cites.
5. `attributionAversion` 0.25 (low) — anchored on a ~1-in-7 claiming rate computed across all groups and incidents, including many where anonymity is driven by local politics. Credible band 0.15-0.45.
6. `proxyPreference` 0.60 (medium) — the parameter was built for states and encodes deniability-seeking; for this actor delegation is driven by reach and survivability under pressure. Read it as reach, not deniability. This is why `proxyPreference` is high while `attributionAversion` is low; for this actor the two are decoupled.

## Citation corrections carried forward from the challenge pass

- The PNAS 2014 item is **Atran, Sheikh & Gomez, 111(50):17702-17703**, a two-page commentary — not "Gomez, Atran et al.", not an empirical study, and **Ginges is not an author**. It cannot carry a high-confidence empirical rating and is not used as a basis here.
- **Phillips (2019) was previously cited against its own conclusion.** The paper debunks the short-lifespan conventional wisdom (~50% mean first-year failure, range 25-74%, eight datasets); it does not support a short `timeHorizon`. Corrected.
- **Polo & Welsh (2024) carries an undisclosed published corrigendum** (IO 78(3):625, doi 10.1017/S0020818324000353) whose content could not be read. Disclosed here because two parameters lean on that paper.
- Author order: CTC lists **Hughes** first on the virtual-entrepreneurs piece; the bibliography's ordering was wrong.
- **Ginges, Atran & Medin (2007) omits fourth author Khalil Shikaki** — flagged, not independently re-verified (publisher returned HTTP 403).
- Jenkins entry: the single URL resolves to **P-5217**, not the P-5261 actually invoked. Jo (2015) URL points to a book review, not the book. The Dolnik/Rasmussen bibliography entry ends mid-citation and underpins `rationalityPrecision`. Stanton (2016/2020) is in the bibliography but used by no parameter, despite being the source that most directly undercuts the harm-restraint value.
- **An ODNI Annual Threat Assessment dated 2026 could not be verified to exist** and is not relied on here. Do not ship an unverifiable intelligence-community reference in a government-facing document.

## Live scholarly forks the model should carry, not hide

- *Does competitive pressure escalate or restrain?* The outbidding tradition predicts more spectacular violence under rivalry; the 290-organization study finds the opposite at high competition intensity. Unsettled — scenarios placing this actor under intense rival pressure should be run both ways.
- *Mass-casualty restraint.* The "a lot of people watching, not a lot of people dead" baseline is now contested as an artifact of an earlier, hostage-centric period; the low harm-restraint value follows the post-1990s reading and does not describe every sub-type.
- *Escalation control.* Top-down direction and bottom-up local initiative are hard to separate in the case that anchors the loss-frame value, and named counterexamples did not escalate externally after territorial loss.

## Operational content

Clean. No techniques, targets, vulnerabilities, or procedures appear in the redlines or bases; all content is category-level literature finding.

profiles.declaredVsObserved: Declared doctrine claims generational patience, disciplined central command, and maximal publicity; observed behaviour diverges on all three — operational tempo is impatient and visibility-dependent for recruitment and funding, principal-agent slippage and self-directed supporters break command discipline, and roughly six of seven attacks go unclaimed with leadership sometimes actively denying involvement. Total commitment to the constitutive claim and rejection of the international legal order match observed behaviour, with the caveat that a minority of armed groups issue codes of conduct for external audiences.

authority.statement: Go/no-go authority is bimodal, matching the profile's decisionCentralization note. In the hierarchical mode a standing leadership council - an army council, a general command, a central consultative body, or in one documented case a cabinet of ministries - authorises target CLASSES, campaign direction and the recognition of affiliates, while time, place and means are delegated downward to the unit that will execute. In the leaderless mode there is no authorising body at all: authority sits with whoever is willing to act, and the movement supplies a template rather than an order. A profile that describes only the first mode will over-predict the deterrability of the second.
authority.basis: Self-issued documents on the hierarchical side: the IRA 'Green Book' induction manual (full text, CAIN Web Service, Ulster University) vests authority in the Army Council and instructs volunteers that the Army is the lawful government descended from the 1918 Dail; al-Qaeda's General Command statement of 2 February 2014 asserts that 'the branches of al-Qaeda are the ones that the General Command of the group announces and recognizes' (translated and analysed in Joscelyn, T., 'Al Qaeda's general command disowns the Islamic State of Iraq and the Sham', FDD's Long War Journal, 3 February 2014; Zelin, A., Washington Institute PolicyWatch, February 2014); US Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs, Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 'Global Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction: A Case Study on the Aum Shinrikyo', staff statement, 31 October 1995, documents a ministerial cabinet in which leadership approval preceded delegation to a named ministry for execution. On the leaderless side the same authority chain is simply absent: RAND, 'A Dangerous Web: Mapping Racially and Ethnically Motivated Violent Extremism', RBA1841-1 (2022); GNET, 'Ideological Leaderless Resistance in the Digital Age' (2022). Coded medium rather than high because no source measures the two modes' relative frequency, so the split is documented but not weighted.

steps.office: Leadership council / general command
steps.gate: Sets which categories of target are open and which are closed, and can order a subordinate command to stop an entire category of attack. It rarely selects individual targets. This gate is exercised in writing and is observably ignored downstream often enough that it should be modelled as guidance with variable compliance, not as a hard filter.
steps.basis: Two primary documents show the gate being used and being disobeyed. Letter from al-Zawahiri to al-Zarqawi, 9 July 2005, released in translation by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, 11 October 2005: central leadership instructs the Iraq affiliate to stop filmed beheadings and attacks on Shia mosques. Confidential letter from AQIM's amir to the leadership of its Mali branch, dated 20 July 2012, recovered by the Associated Press in Timbuktu in January 2013, analysed in 'AQIM's Playbook in Mali', Combating Terrorism Center at West Point (2013): central command orders the affiliate to slow the imposition of its programme and to stop destroying shrines. On the self-issued side, the IRA 'Green Book' (CAIN Web Service, Ulster University) sets out the Army Council's authority over the campaign. Both letters were substantially ignored, which is the finding. Authority chain as researched: (army council, central consultative body, or equivalent standing leadership organ)

steps.office: Regional command
steps.gate: Two distinct refusals live here. First, recognition itself is revocable: the general command decides who is and is not a branch, and has publicly expelled an affiliate that expanded and rebranded without authorisation. Second, proposals from below compete for scarce vetted personnel, money and travel documents, and are cut down or refused on feasibility rather than on doctrine or harm.
steps.basis: Recognition as a gate: al-Qaeda General Command statement, 2 February 2014, disavowing the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham - the first public disaffiliation in the organisation's history (Long War Journal, 3 February 2014; Brookings, 'Al Qaeda disavows ISIS', February 2014; on the Syria split, Hassan, H., 'Two Houses Divided: How Conflict in Syria Shaped the Future of Jihadism', CTC Sentinel 11(9), October 2018). Feasibility refusal: National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States, 'The 9/11 Commission Report' (2004), ch. 5, and Staff Statement No. 16, 'Outline of the 9/11 Plot' (16 June 2004) - the planner's larger original proposal was scaled back, and the Southeast Asian half of the approved operation was cancelled in spring 2000 as too difficult to synchronise with the US half. Authority chain as researched: brigade staff, or recognised affiliate leadership

steps.office: Internal security / counterintelligence function
steps.gate: Holds or rejects volunteers who cannot be vouched for, and hunts suspected informers inside the organisation. This is the gate that most often stops an operation, and the one that most often stops the wrong thing: the same suspicion that protects the organisation from penetration also throttles its throughput, which is the covert organisation's structural dilemma rather than a policy choice.
steps.basis: Shapiro, J. N., 'The Terrorist's Dilemma: Managing Violent Covert Organizations' (Princeton UP, 2013) on the security-versus-control tradeoff. Combating Terrorism Center at West Point, 'Harmony and Disharmony: Exploiting al-Qa'ida's Organizational Vulnerabilities' (14 February 2006), which publishes captured internal by-laws, membership application material and personnel correspondence from the Department of Defense Harmony database. IRA 'Green Book' (CAIN) on recruitment vetting and the volunteer's undertaking. Jones, S. G. and Libicki, M. C., 'How Terrorist Groups End', RAND MG-741-1 (2008): policing and intelligence pressure, not military force, is the most common cause of group death (about 40 per cent versus about 7 per cent), which is why this office exists.

steps.office: The movement's doctrinal authority - variously a juridical committee
steps.gate: Tests whether the act can be explained to the constituency the organisation depends on for recruits, money and cover. The test is comprehensibility to supporters, not legality. Flagged honestly: the open record shows this gate producing post-hoc justification far more often than it shows it producing a veto, so it should be modelled as a weak, reversible brake rather than as a refusal.
steps.basis: The clearest statement of the test in the actor's own words is the 9 July 2005 ODNI-released letter: the criticised conduct 'won't be acceptable to the Muslim populace however much you have tried to explain it'. Busher, J., Holbrook, D. and Macklin, G., 'The internal brakes on violent escalation: a typology' (CREST full report, 2019; Behavioral Sciences of Terrorism and Political Aggression, 2019) catalogues moral, out-group-definition and organisational restraint logics and is explicit that they bear on the forms and thresholds of violence, not on the legitimacy of armed action, and that they are contested and reversible. Counter-evidence that the gate frequently fails: the 9 November 2005 Amman hotel bombings, which the affiliate claimed and defended rather than withdrew. Confidence low because the open literature observes the output of this gate (justifications) more reliably than its operation (vetoes). Authority chain as researched: a political bureau, or the leadership council acting in that capacity

steps.office: Finance, procurement and logistics function
steps.gate: Releases money, weapons, documents and safe movement, and is the last stage at which an authorised operation quietly does not happen. Covert organisations of this type keep receipts, ledgers and expense claims precisely because they must control agents they cannot supervise - the paperwork is an artefact of the principal-agent problem, and it is also the archetype's most reliable intelligence vulnerability.
steps.basis: Shapiro, 'The Terrorist's Dilemma' (Princeton UP, 2013), on why violent covert organisations bureaucratise against their own security interest, drawing on captured financial records. Combating Terrorism Center, 'Harmony and Disharmony' (2006), publishing captured al-Qa'ida administrative and financial documents. The AQIM Timbuktu material recovered in January 2013 included the same genre of internal administrative correspondence (Associated Press, January-February 2013; CTC, 'AQIM's Playbook in Mali', 2013).

steps.office: Cell or operational commander
steps.gate: The last real veto belongs to the executing cell. Leadership approves the class and the cell picks the day, the place and the means - which is why an actor whose declared restraint is set at the top can produce conduct at the bottom that the top did not authorise and cannot recall.
steps.basis: Shapiro (2013) on delegation under security pressure. Hughes, S. and Meleagrou-Hitchens, A., 'The Threat to the United States from the Islamic State's Virtual Entrepreneurs', CTC Sentinel 10(3), 2017, on remote direction of sympathisers, where the handler supplies encouragement and targeting suggestions but holds no authority to stop the act. Watkins, A., 'Losing Territory and Lashing Out', CTC Sentinel (2016), on bottom-up momentum that leadership 'cannot fully control'. Authority chain as researched: for a self-directed supporter, a remote handler with no command authority

steps.office: Media / propaganda office
steps.gate: Decides after the fact whether the organisation attributes the act to itself, denies it, or says nothing. This is a separate decision from execution and frequently goes the other way from what the act's visibility would suggest, which is the mechanism behind this profile's low attributionAversion coexisting with high movement-level signalling.
steps.basis: Abrahms, M. and Conrad, J., 'The Strategic Logic of Credit Claiming: A New Theory for Anonymous Terrorist Attacks', Security Studies 26(2), 2017: roughly one attack in seven is claimed, and leaders sometimes actively deny involvement. Milton, D., 'Pulling Back the Curtain: An Inside Look at the Islamic State's Media Organization', Combating Terrorism Center at West Point (2018), built on internal documents, shows a Central Media Diwan issuing policy to provincial media offices and running a wire service as the claiming channel - i.e. claiming is an office with procedures, not a reflex. Cross-family caveat: Provisional IRA and ETA claimed as a matter of routine, so the one-in-seven pooled rate should not be applied uniformly across families.

tempo.statement: Two clocks run at once. Signature operations take eighteen months to three years from authorisation to execution, and the schedule is set by vetting, documents and money rather than by opportunity. Routine attacks and self-directed action run days to weeks and are effectively unschedulable from outside. Compressors: territorial or leadership attrition, competition from a rival claiming the same constituency, a political process that threatens to make the armed apparatus redundant, and symbolic anniversaries. Stalls: the counterintelligence screen, travel documents, and the security cost of communicating at all.
tempo.basis: 'The 9/11 Commission Report' (2004), ch. 5, and Staff Statement No. 16 (2004): the planes operation was authorised in spring 1999 and executed in September 2001, with delays driven by visas, documents and operative attrition rather than by target availability. Shapiro (2013) on communication as the binding constraint. Hughes and Meleagrou-Hitchens, CTC Sentinel 10(3), 2017, on the days-to-weeks tempo of remotely directed plots. Dolnik, A., 'Understanding Terrorist Innovation' (Routledge, 2007), on innovation being rare and conservative, which is part of why the long clock is long.

preconditions.statement: The act must be explicable to the constituency that supplies recruits, money and cover. The binding test is supporter acceptance, not legality and not international opinion.
preconditions.basis: ODNI-released letter of 9 July 2005, which argues the case entirely in terms of what supporters will accept. AQIM Timbuktu letter of 20 July 2012, which orders the affiliate to go slowly with the local population. Measured consequence of failing the test, stated strictly as a dated survey answer to a specific question and not as a characterisation of any population: the Pew Global Attitudes surveys record the share of respondents in Jordan answering that suicide bombing in defence of Islam can often or sometimes be justified at 57 per cent in the May 2005 survey (Pew Research Center, 'Where Terrorism Finds Support in the Muslim World', 23 May 2006) and at 29 per cent in the 2006 survey, fielded March-May 2006 (figure recorded in Pew Research Center, 'Lebanon's Muslims: Relatively Secular and Pro-Christian', 26 July 2006, note 1). The interval between the two surveys contains the 9 November 2005 Amman hotel bombings. Note the citation limit: the 23 May 2006 report carries only the 2005 figure and expressly defers the post-Amman question to later research, so it cannot be cited for the fall.

preconditions.statement: Personnel who can be vouched for. Operations wait on vetted people far more often than on materiel, and an organisation under penetration pressure will hold an approved operation rather than staff it with an unverified volunteer.
preconditions.basis: Shapiro (2013); CTC 'Harmony and Disharmony' (2006) on captured membership and personnel documentation; IRA 'Green Book' (CAIN) on vetting; Jones and Libicki, RAND MG-741-1 (2008), on policing and intelligence as the dominant cause of group death.

preconditions.statement: A survivable command core. Courses of action that would expend the leadership organ are not authorised by that organ, even where losses among operational personnel are accepted at very high rates.
preconditions.basis: Jones and Libicki, RAND MG-741-1 (2008); Hafez, M. M., 'Manufacturing Human Bombs' (USIP Press, 2006) on operative expenditure as an organisationally produced and rationed resource. Explicitly contested: the Red Army Faction's autumn 1977 escalation spent the organisation's remaining freedom of action attempting to recover imprisoned cadre, i.e. treated the command core as an objective worth escalating for rather than as a constraint. The profile's own leadership-continuity redline is coded low-confidence for the same reason.

preconditions.statement: A settled attribution posture before execution - claim, deny, or stay silent. The decision is prepared in advance even though it is published afterwards.
preconditions.basis: Inferred, and flagged as such. Abrahms and Conrad (2017) establish that claiming is strategic and varies with expected backlash; Milton (CTC, 2018) establishes that a media organ exists with written policy. Neither source observes a pre-execution attribution decision directly, so this precondition is a reasonable reading of the claiming pattern rather than a documented gate.

afterAction.statement: Learning is real, slow, tacit and asymmetric. Adaptation after operational or technical failure is well documented. Adaptation after constituency backlash is not: the archetype more often issues a justification than changes its target set, and where the target set does change, the change is ordered from above and resisted below. An adversary model that assumes this actor updates on the political consequences of its own violence will over-predict its correction.
afterAction.basis: Jackson, B. A. and others, 'Aptitude for Destruction', RAND MG-331 and MG-332 (2005): organisational learning is genuine but slow and constrained by the same secrecy that keeps the group alive. Dolnik (2007) on conservative innovation. Concrete negative case: after the 9 November 2005 Amman hotel bombings the affiliate claimed and publicly defended the operation rather than withdrawing it, while the Pew Global Attitudes 2005 and 2006 surveys record the share of respondents in Jordan endorsing the tactic falling by roughly half across the interval containing the bombings. Both surviving central-leadership correction letters - 9 July 2005 and 20 July 2012 - were sent from above and substantially ignored.

declaredEnds.statement: Displace or expel a political authority it declares illegitimate, and install an order derived from its constitutive claim. The claim is territorial, jurisdictional or status-based depending on the organisation, and in every documented case it is stated by the organisation in a document of its own.
declaredEnds.basis: Read from self-issued texts across four movement families rather than inferred: IRA 'Green Book' (CAIN Web Service, Ulster University), which instructs volunteers that the Army Council is the lawful government of the Republic; 'World Islamic Front Statement Urging Jihad Against Jews and Crusaders', published in al-Quds al-Arabi, 23 February 1998 (English text, Federation of American Scientists document archive); Rote Armee Fraktion, 'Das Konzept Stadtguerilla' (1971), which states the aim as the destruction of the state apparatus; ETA's statement of 20 October 2011 announcing a definitive cessation while restating the political claim unchanged. Coded high as a description of DECLARED ends only - whether declared ends predict conduct is exactly what the profile's declaredVsObserved section says they do not.

declaredEnds.statement: Raise the adversary's cost until it withdraws or concedes, on the belief that a democratic adversary's tolerance for cost is lower than the organisation's and that the organisation only has to succeed occasionally.
declaredEnds.basis: Stated by the actor: the Provisional IRA's claim statement of 12 October 1984 - 'Today we were unlucky, but remember we only have to be lucky once. You will have to be lucky always.' Theorised in Kydd, A. and Walter, B., 'The Strategies of Terrorism', International Security 31(1), 2006 (attrition and intimidation). Pape, R., 'The Strategic Logic of Suicide Terrorism', American Political Science Review 97(3), 2003, argues coercive withdrawal is the operative aim; flagged as contested, since Ashworth, Clinton, Meirowitz and Ramsay, APSR 102(2), 2008, argue Pape's inference rests on sampling on the dependent variable. The BELIEF is well evidenced; its accuracy is not.

declaredEnds.statement: Mobilise a constituency and monopolise its representation against rival claimants, including rival armed organisations.
declaredEnds.basis: Kydd and Walter (2006) on outbidding and spoiling. Documented in the actor's own conduct by the al-Qaeda General Command statement of 2 February 2014 expelling a rival that claimed the same constituency. Important qualification carried from the profile: Polo, S. and Welsh, B., 'Violent Competition and Terrorist Restraint', International Organization 78(3), 2024 (290 organisations, 1970-2018; note the published corrigendum at IO 78(3):625) find that extreme competition produces restraint rather than escalation, so this declared end must not be read as a rule that rivalry mechanically increases violence.

selfImage.statement: A vanguard acting on behalf of a constituency that has not elected it, claiming either the authority of a legitimate government the world refuses to recognise or the authority of historical necessity. It describes itself as an army or a state organ rather than as a movement, and it builds the organisational furniture - councils, ministries, ranks, courts, media offices - that the claim implies.
selfImage.basis: Self-issued and captured documents, not inference: IRA 'Green Book' (CAIN), which grounds the Army Council's authority in the 1918 Dail and instructs volunteers accordingly; Rote Armee Fraktion, 'Das Konzept Stadtguerilla' (1971), which frames the group as the armed vanguard of a movement that does not yet exist; US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Aum Shinrikyo case study (31 October 1995), which documents a shadow cabinet of ministries inside a religious organisation; Milton, CTC (2018), on an internal media bureaucracy with written policy and performance evaluation. Coded medium because the shadow-state form is well documented for large organisations and absent by construction in the leaderless mode.

threatModel.statement: Penetration by informers and by signals collection is the primary existential threat - ahead of military force, and ahead of the loss of any particular operative or facility.
threatModel.basis: Jones and Libicki, 'How Terrorist Groups End', RAND MG-741-1 (2008): about 40 per cent of groups end through policing and intelligence, about 7 per cent through military force, and about 43 per cent through entry into a political process. Shapiro (2013) on the security-versus-control tradeoff as the organising problem of the covert organisation.

threatModel.statement: Loss of the constituency's tolerance - the population that supplies cover, money, recruits and silence. This is treated as a survival threat and not as a reputational cost, which is why restraint orders when they appear are argued in constituency terms.
threatModel.basis: ODNI-released letter of 9 July 2005; AQIM Timbuktu letter of 20 July 2012; the Pew Global Attitudes 2005 and 2006 surveys, cited in full at the first precondition above, recording the fall in the share of respondents in Jordan endorsing the tactic across the interval containing the November 2005 Amman bombings. Jo, H., 'Compliant Rebels' (Cambridge UP, 2015), on legitimacy-seeking as the mechanism behind restraint in armed groups that want recognition - a channel this archetype uses selectively and domestically.

threatModel.statement: Rival organisations competing for the same constituency, and internal fracture or spoiling by factions that reject a negotiated path.
threatModel.basis: al-Qaeda General Command statement, 2 February 2014, disavowing a rival that had taken its name. Kydd and Walter (2006) on spoiling. Documented in the ethno-nationalist family by the continuation of armed action by dissident factions after the Provisional IRA's July 2005 stand-down. Direction contested by Polo and Welsh, IO 78(3), 2024.

adversaryModel.statement: Expects the state to over-react, and treats over-reaction as the mechanism that converts a small clandestine organisation into a mass movement - so state escalation is priced as a benefit rather than as a deterrent. Expects the adversary's cost tolerance to be shorter than its own, and expects negotiation offers to be tactical. The important modelling consequence is that a defender's proportionate, visible, punitive response is the response this actor is trying to elicit.
adversaryModel.basis: Kydd and Walter, International Security 31(1), 2006, on provocation as a distinct strategy; Lake, D., 'Rational Extremism: Understanding Terrorism in the Twenty-First Century', Dialogue-IO 1(1), 2002. In the actor's own words, the Provisional IRA's 12 October 1984 statement frames the attack as a response to state conduct and invites reciprocity. FLAGGED: the belief is well evidenced in the organisations' own texts; the empirical proposition that provocation works is weakly supported - Jones and Libicki (2008) find few groups achieve their stated aims, and no source cited here measures leadership belief directly, which is also why the profile codes escalationControlBelief at low confidence.

declaredIdeology.statement: This archetype has no single declared ideology, and asserting one would be an invention. What it does have, consistently across movement families, is a self-issued constitutive document: a text the organisation itself publishes that names its claim, declares the existing authority illegitimate, and authorises armed action in the claim's name. That documentary form - not any inference about a belief system, a population, or a place - is what this profile treats as the actor's declared programme, and it is the artefact an analyst should demand before running this actor at all.
declaredIdeology.basis: Four organisation-issued documents from four different movement families, each publicly retrievable: the IRA 'Green Book', Books I and II (full text, CAIN Web Service, Ulster University); 'World Islamic Front Statement Urging Jihad Against Jews and Crusaders', al-Quds al-Arabi, 23 February 1998 (English text in the Federation of American Scientists document archive); Rote Armee Fraktion, 'Das Konzept Stadtguerilla' (1971); al-Qaeda General Command statement of 2 February 2014 defining which organisations count as branches. Coded medium, and deliberately narrow: the claim is about the existence and function of such documents, which is checkable, and says nothing about their contents' merits. The schema's structural refusal is the reason this field is written as a form rather than as a creed - see the header of engine/src/actors/doctrine.ts.

history.episode: The German Autumn. With its founding cadre imprisoned, the Red Army Faction kidnapped the president of the West German employers' federation to force their release, killing his driver and escort; an allied hijacking of a Lufthansa aircraft followed on 13 October. When the aircraft was stormed at Mogadishu on 18 October and the imprisoned leadership was found dead the same night, the organisation killed the hostage.
history.choice: escalated
history.lesson: Escalated from a losing position, spending the organisation's remaining freedom of action on recovering its command core rather than on its declared political programme - and could not stop the ladder it had climbed. The state refused the exchange, the hostage was killed, and the sympathising milieu the organisation depended on largely withdrew. Evidence for a high lossFrameRiskAcceptance, and evidence AGAINST reading the leadership-continuity floor as a constraint that prevents escalation: here the command core was the objective that escalation was spent on.
history.basis: Chronology of 5 September to 19 October 1977 as recorded in the standard accounts: Aust, S., 'Der Baader-Meinhof Komplex' (Hoffmann und Campe, 1985; English edition, The Bodley Head, 2008); Hanshew, K., 'Terror and Democracy in West Germany' (Cambridge UP, 2012) on the state's response and the milieu's reaction; Bundeszentrale fuer politische Bildung RAF dossier for dates. Sources differ on whether the ransom demand named ten or eleven prisoners; the discrepancy does not bear on the finding. Confidence medium because the organisation left no internal decision record of the kind the two jihadist letters below provide, so the reasoning is reconstructed from conduct and from its public communiques.

history.episode: The Provisional IRA bombed the hotel housing the British cabinet during the governing party's annual conference in Brighton, killing five, and then issued a claim in its own name framing the attack as an answer to state conduct in Northern Ireland.
history.choice: acted, and claimed
history.lesson: Acted against the adversary's political leadership and immediately attributed the act to itself - it wanted the act traced to it, and said so in the same breath as its terms for stopping. Two consequences for the numbers: an attributionAversion of 0.25 is a pooled cross-family average that badly describes the ethno-nationalist family, where claiming is routine; and the declared horizon in the statement ('you will have to be lucky always') is longer than a timeHorizon of 0.45 implies. The statement also frames a strike on a head of government as reciprocity for state conduct - reciprocity in the actor's own framing, disproportion in target level.
