history.basis: IRA statement of 12 October 1984, widely reproduced in contemporaneous reporting and in the UK National Archives' Brighton bomb commentary: 'Mrs Thatcher will now realise that Britain cannot occupy our country and torture our prisoners and shoot our people in their own streets and get away with it. Today we were unlucky, but remember we only have to be lucky once. You will have to be lucky always.' Read against Abrahms and Conrad, Security Studies 26(2), 2017, whose roughly one-in-seven claiming rate this case cuts against by family.

history.episode: Aum Shinrikyo released sarin from containers placed on five Tokyo subway trains timed to converge on the government district at rush hour, and then publicly denied responsibility, its leadership claiming the organisation had itself been gassed and that its chemical stocks were for legitimate manufacturing.
history.choice: acted, then refused attribution
history.lesson: Acted at the floor of harm restraint against an undifferentiated civilian target set, and then declined to claim. This is the cleanest available demonstration that mass-casualty intent and attribution-seeking are separable channels: a low counterpartHarmRestraint does not imply a high claiming propensity, which is exactly the reconciliation the profile's signalingPreference basis is forced into. The organisation's own ministerial structure shows the operation was approved at the top and delegated for execution rather than improvised, so this is a hierarchical-mode data point.
history.basis: US Senate Committee on Governmental Affairs, Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, staff statement 'Global Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction: A Case Study on the Aum Shinrikyo', 31 October 1995: attack description; the ministerial structure and the sequence in which leadership approval preceded delegation for execution; the 24 March 1995 public denial and the assessment by chemical experts that the explanation offered was 'not believable'. Casualty figures vary across sources - the Senate report states twelve killed and about 5,500 injured; later summaries give thirteen or fourteen as further victims died. Family caveat: this is the only apocalyptic/new-religious-movement case in the dossier and the profile's parameters were not calibrated on it.

history.episode: Al-Qaeda's leadership cancelled the Southeast Asian half of an already-approved simultaneous-hijacking operation in spring 2000, having earlier cut down the operation planner's larger original proposal.
history.choice: declined
history.lesson: Refused an approved operation on synchronisation grounds - a top-level veto exercised on feasibility, not on harm and not on legitimacy. Evidence that in the hierarchical mode authority over scope genuinely sits at the top and is used to shrink operations as well as to launch them, and evidence that leadership BELIEVES it controls the shape of what it launches. It is not evidence that the belief is accurate, which is the distinction the profile's escalationControlBelief basis turns on.
history.basis: National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States, 'The 9/11 Commission Report' (2004), ch. 5; Staff Statement No. 16, 'Outline of the 9/11 Plot' (16 June 2004): the Southeast Asia portion was cancelled in spring 2000 because it would be too difficult to coordinate with the US portion, and the planner's original, larger proposal had already been scaled back. Material qualification: the Commission's reconstruction of the planning sequence rests substantially on detainee reporting whose reliability the Commission itself qualifies in its notes, so 'high' here means well-documented in the public record, not independently corroborated.

history.episode: Al-Qaeda's central leadership sent written instructions to its Iraq affiliate to stop filmed beheadings of hostages and attacks on Shia mosques, arguing explicitly that supporters could not be brought to accept them however they were explained.
history.choice: held - ordered restraint on a target class
history.lesson: Ordered restraint in writing, on a target class, for constituency-legitimacy reasons rather than moral ones - and was substantially ignored: the affiliate continued and four months later bombed three hotels in Amman. Two findings. First, a restraint gate exists in this archetype and it is a legitimacy calculation. Second, the legitimacy channel that binds this actor is constituency acceptance, not the international-legal legitimacy that the 0.15 legitimacyWeight scalar measures - a simulation reading that scalar as global legitimacy indifference will miss the only restraint lever the record shows being pulled.
history.basis: Letter from al-Zawahiri to al-Zarqawi, dated 9 July 2005, released in English translation by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence on 11 October 2005 (text mirrored at the Federation of American Scientists and GlobalSecurity document archives): 'this matter won't be acceptable to the Muslim populace however much you have tried to explain it, and aversion to this will continue.' Load-bearing caveat: authenticity was publicly disputed at the time - see Jamestown Foundation, 'Is al-Zawahiri's Letter to al-Zarqawi a Fake?', Terrorism Focus (2005) - and the affiliate denied the letter existed. Confidence is medium for that reason, not because the content is ambiguous.

history.episode: The Provisional IRA's Army Council ordered all units to dump arms and end the armed campaign after thirty-six years, following an internal consultation of units and volunteers, and authorised its representative to put the arsenal verifiably beyond use; an independent commission reported the decommissioning complete on 26 September 2005.
history.choice: stood down, and disarmed
history.lesson: Held, and then surrendered the armed apparatus, under sustained attrition and infiltration rather than escalating - a direct counter-case to the loss-frame escalation reading that anchors lossFrameRiskAcceptance at 0.75, and consistent instead with the competition-produces-restraint finding. It is also the counter-case the profile's own 'armed capability is never surrendered' redline names, which is why that redline is scoped to a months-to-few-years horizon rather than asserted absolutely. The order was issued centrally and obeyed, which is what high decisionCentralization in the hierarchical mode is supposed to predict. Scope limit: the Army Council's writ, not the movement's - dissident factions continued armed action.
history.basis: 'Irish Republican Army (IRA) Statement on the Ending of the Armed Campaign', 28 July 2005, full text in the CAIN Web Service archive, Ulster University: 'All IRA units have been ordered to dump arms', with volunteers instructed to pursue the political programme by exclusively peaceful means and the decision taken after an internal consultation process. Independent International Commission on Decommissioning, statement read at a press conference in Belfast, 26 September 2005 (transcript, CAIN): the commission concluded with confidence that the arms decommissioned represented the totality of the arsenal.

history.episode: ETA detonated a van bomb in a car park at Madrid-Barajas airport during the ceasefire it had itself declared in March 2006, having telephoned warnings to three recipients about an hour beforehand. Two people asleep in the car park were killed, the negotiation track collapsed, and the organisation claimed the attack on 9 January 2007 and declared the ceasefire over on 5 June 2007.
history.choice: escalated, with its own harm-limiting procedure failing
history.lesson: Acted while formally in ceasefire, using a warning-call procedure designed to produce property damage and political signal without deaths. Two findings the flat 0.2 counterpartHarmRestraint cannot carry: this archetype does operate documented internal harm-limiting procedures, and those procedures fail, so restraint here is a real but unreliable mechanism rather than an absent trait. It also shows a ceasefire being treated as tactical and reversible, which is the half of the profile's armed-capability redline that holds even in the family that supplies the redline's main counter-case.
history.basis: ETA declared a ceasefire in March 2006; the Terminal 4 car park bombing at Madrid-Barajas on 30 December 2006 killed two Ecuadorian nationals and injured dozens despite warning calls made roughly an hour before detonation; ETA claimed the attack on 9 January 2007 and announced the ceasefire over on 5 June 2007 (contemporaneous BBC News reporting, 30 December 2006 and 5 June 2007; Spanish court convictions of three members, 2010). Context and the negotiation track: Whitfield, T., 'The Basque Conflict and ETA: The Difficulties of an Ending', United States Institute of Peace Special Report 384 (2016). Confidence medium: the intent behind the warning calls is inferred from the procedure and from the organisation's subsequent statements, not from an internal document.

history.episode: AQIM's central command sent written guidance to the leadership of its Mali branch ordering it to slow the imposition of its programme, to stop destroying shrines and applying corporal punishment to the local population, and to avoid provoking foreign military intervention. The branch did not comply; France intervened in January 2013.
history.choice: ordered restraint; control failed
history.lesson: Held at the centre and acted at the edge. The leadership's own document shows it believed it could time and throttle an affiliate's conduct; the affiliate's behaviour shows it could not. This is the clearest open-source case for the profile's central reading that DECLARED escalation control exceeds DEMONSTRATED control - and for reading proxyPreference as reach rather than deniability, since the affiliate was never plausibly deniable, only distant and unbiddable.
history.basis: Confidential letter from AQIM's amir to the leadership of its Mali branch, dated 20 July 2012, recovered by Associated Press journalists in a house in Timbuktu in January 2013 and published in translation; analysed in 'AQIM's Playbook in Mali', Combating Terrorism Center at West Point (2013), and revisited in 'Revisiting the Mali al-Qa'ida Playbook: How the Group is Advancing on its Goals in the Sahel', CTC (2019). See also Guidere, M., 'The Timbuktu Letters: New Insights about AQIM', Res Militaris 4(1), 2014 (open-access deposit hal-01081769), for provenance discussion. Provenance caveat driving the medium confidence: this is a leave-behind document recovered by journalists, not a chain-of-custody exhibit, and the corpus's completeness is unknown.

history.episode: An individual with no organisational chain of command attacked two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, killing 51, livestreaming the attack and publishing a document immediately beforehand. The national inquiry concluded he acted alone and examined his radicalisation through online material rather than through any organisation.
history.choice: acted, with no institution to authorise it
history.lesson: Demonstrates the archetype's second mode, in which none of the gates above exist: no council authorised the target class, no security function vetted the actor, no finance office released resources, and no media office decided the claim - the actor self-attributed in real time. Evidence that decisionCentralization is genuinely bimodal and that a mid value describes no real organisation; in this mode attribution aversion is effectively zero while signalling is maximal, the opposite corner from the 1995 case above. This is also the movement family the profile flags as informing no parameter at all, so the episode is offered as the gap rather than as a calibration.
history.basis: Royal Commission of Inquiry into the terrorist attack on Christchurch masjidain on 15 March 2019, 'Ko to tatou kainga tenei', report presented 26 November 2020 and publicly released 8 December 2020 (Government of New Zealand), which found the individual acted alone and reviewed his use of online platforms; RAND, 'A Dangerous Web: Mapping Racially and Ethnically Motivated Violent Extremism', RBA1841-1 (2022), and GNET, 'Ideological Leaderless Resistance in the Digital Age' (2022), on movement structures with no authorising body. Contested detail, disclosed: later archival research by a University of Auckland team identified extensive prior imageboard posting by the attacker that the Commission's account under-weighted - 'Christchurch terrorist discussed attacks online a year before carrying them out, new research reveals', The Conversation, 20 February 2024, and 'Christchurch attacks 5 years on: terrorist's online history gives clues to preventing future atrocities', The Conversation, 13 March 2024; peer-reviewed version, 'The Role of Ideology in Motivating Lone Actor Terrorism: An Analysis of the Online Record of the Christchurch Terrorist' (University of Auckland research deposit, 2025) - so the inquiry's radicalisation findings are the best public record but not the last word. The perpetrator is deliberately not named and no method detail is recorded here.

weakestClaim.finding: the justification-review gate (confidence: low). The open literature reliably observes this gate's OUTPUT (post-hoc justifications) but almost never observes it exercising a veto, so it is coded as a weak, reversible brake rather than a filter. Second weakest: procedure.preconditions[3] (pre-execution attribution posture), which is inferred from claiming patterns rather than documented as a gate.

profiles.label: State-aligned proxy network
profiles.summary: This is an archetype prior over a family of delegated armed organizations — territorially governing insurgents, expedient militias, contractor forces, and cyber front organizations — not a portrait of one organization, and its parameters are midpoints over sub-types that genuinely differ. It decides fast, either through a small commander circle or through a fragmented set of independent go-nodes, with no legal-review body and no bureaucratic veto, producing a low-precision, high-variance process in which a sponsor's preferences reach it through a lossy channel rather than as orders. Because its operating resources come from outside the local population, the institutional incentive to court that population is weak and restraint on harm to noncombatants is correspondingly low, reversing only where the organization is actively seeking recognition or governs a constituency it depends on materially. It absorbs heavy personnel and materiel loss but is acutely sensitive to costs that threaten the organization itself, and it answers coercive discipline — including discipline from its own patron — with defection and escalation rather than compliance.

ownCostTolerance.basis: DOWNGRADED from 0.75. Krieg & Rickli 2019 and Salehyan 2010 establish that the SPONSOR externalizes cost — a principal-side proposition that does not by itself measure the agent's own tolerance. Agent-side evidence cuts both ways: Popovic 2017 (TPV 29:5) shows agents facing organizational cost defect rather than absorb; Karlen 2017 (JPR 54:4) shows dependence on terminable support. Observed: high tolerance for personnel/materiel loss; low tolerance for costs that threaten the organization itself (see redline 1).

counterpartHarmRestraint.basis: Salehyan, Siroky & Wood 2014 (International Organization 68:3, 633-661) — external funding reduces the need to extract resources from, and therefore court, the population, raising one-sided violence; multiple principals restrain less; principals that are democratic or exposed to human-rights lobbies restrain MORE (the paper's variable is human-rights sensitivity, not autocracy per se). CONDITIONAL, not a point fact: Jo 2015 shows territory-governing, legitimacy-seeking groups comply materially more. Widen to 0.45-0.60 for governing/legitimacy-seeking agents, 0.15-0.25 for expedient agents with a rights-insensitive principal. Note out-of-sample risk: the 2014 finding is estimated on civil-war rebel groups and is being extended to contractor and cyber sub-types where it has not been tested.

attributionAversion.basis: BIMODAL by sub-type — a single point estimate hides the split. Deniability is primarily the SPONSOR's asset (Cormac & Aldrich 2018 on non-acknowledgement). Claiming sub-type (~0.15): Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58 (Mar 2026) documents Houthi claiming of operations, and finds Iran lacks direct command and control over the post-2023 maritime campaign while actions are still ascribed to it. Concealed sub-type (~0.60): front/persona-based cyber proxies (Chatham House 2026; Maurer 2018) where operator concealment is intrinsic. The agent is averse to provable sponsor linkage mainly when the patron makes support conditional on it.

proxyPreference.basis: DOWNGRADED from 0.70 — the prior basis was miscited. Karlen & Rauta, 'Dealers and Brokers in Civil Wars' (International Security 47:4, 2023) documents SPONSOR-side dual delegation through conduit STATES, not agent-side re-delegation; Maurer 2018's delegation/orchestration/sanctioning spectrum likewise measures the state's degree of control, not the agent's preference to work through intermediaries. Agent-level re-delegation (criminal intermediaries, fronts, affiliated personas) is described in Chatham House 2026 and Moghadam & Wyss 2020 (nonstate actors sponsoring local surrogates) but is not systematically estimated. ASSUMED, not established.

escalationControlBelief.basis: This is a BELIEF parameter (declared/internal), deliberately not a behavior. Carson 2018 supports covertness as a genuine escalation limiter but at the STATE level — it is evidence for the sponsor node's belief, and importing it to the agent node repeats the level-of-analysis error the modeling note warns against. Belief is reinforced by repeated unpunished sub-threshold action. OBSERVED CALIBRATION IS POOR and appears to be worsening: Clausen (POMEPS 58, 2026) finds the speed and degree of attribution after October 2023 stand out relative to earlier episodes, and that the agent escalated counter to the patron's preferences. Prior draft cited Mumbai 2008 as 'runaway escalation'; that is wrong as stated — it produced a severe unrealized interstate crisis, not realized escalation to war. The label 'control paradox literature' has no canonical referent; the citable formulations are the substitution/control trade-off (Krieg & Rickli 2019) and the principal-agent control dilemma (Byman & Kreps 2010).

timeHorizon.basis: Bimodal. Territorial/governing agents plan over decades; expedient agents spend access fast because patron support is terminable and value must be demonstrated. CITATION CORRECTED: the termination finding is Karlen, 'Turning off the Taps: The Termination of State Sponsorship' (Terrorism and Political Violence 31:4, 733-758); Karlen 2017 (JPR 54:4, 499-512) is about post-conflict RECURRENCE via residual support structures, not termination, and was misattributed in the prior draft.

decisionCentralization.basis: LEVEL CONVENTION REQUIRED — the scalar is meaningless without stating which node it scores. Single armed faction: ~0.70 (go/no-go with a small commander circle, no legal or bureaucratic veto; fast, high variance). Network of factions under one or more principals: ~0.40 (fragmented authority, competing patrons; Popovic 2017; Salehyan/Siroky/Wood 2014 on multiple principals). 0.50 is the archetype midpoint and should be overridden when the scenario fixes the node.

lossFrameRiskAcceptance.basis: Popovic 2017 (TPV 29:5, 922-942): coercive sponsor discipline — detaining leaders, freezing assets — produces defection and violence against the sponsor rather than compliance; decentralized/factionalized agents defect most. Downgraded from 0.78/medium: this rests on one study's mechanism, and the prior draft's second anchor was wrong (Karlen 2017 JPR is about conflict recurrence after external support, not 'termination triggers new armed mobilization').

legitimacyWeight.basis: DECLARED VS OBSERVED DIVERGE and the prior single value conflated them. Declared: many such actors publicly claim legal standing, sign humanitarian commitments, and seek recognition — declared weight is high. Observed: no treaty-party status, no legal-review apparatus, constituency legitimacy dominates international legal cover. Jo 2015 (Compliant Rebels) shows the observed value is strongly conditional — legitimacy-seeking, territory-governing groups comply materially more; widen to 0.45-0.60 for that sub-type, 0.15-0.25 for expedient/contractor sub-types.

signalingPreference.basis: RE-ANCHORED. Claiming and branding of operations to signal to the constituency, demonstrate value to the patron, and coerce the target: Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58 (Mar 2026), documents Houthi claiming and deliberate internationalization of a campaign. Moghadam & Wyss 2020 (International Security 44:4) supports 'proxies are political actors with their own agendas' but is about NONSTATE sponsors selecting political ancillaries and does not establish credit-claiming behavior — the prior draft over-extended it. Chatham House 2026's characterization of publicity-seeking hacktivist fronts is cited but was NOT independently verified in this review.

reciprocityProportion.basis: ASSUMED, not established — no cited study estimates proportionality of agent retaliation. Inference: demonstrative rather than calibrated response, because the agent has no state escalation-management machinery (Byman & Kreps 2010 describes control tensions, which is adjacent evidence, not evidence of retaliatory proportionality). Absorbs and defers when materially dependent on a patron exercising an active veto; Clausen 2026 shows that veto can fail.

redlines.statement: Will not accept disarmament, dissolution, or integration/subordination into a state's regular forces as the price of any settlement or patronage arrangement; these moves end the organization as an organization and are excluded from its choice set regardless of the material offer attached to them.
redlines.basis: Popovic 2017 (Terrorism and Political Violence 29:5, 922-942): coercive sponsor discipline aimed at forcing submission produces defection rather than compliance, so raising the price moves this commitment the wrong way. Supported by the termination literature under its corrected citation, Karlen, 'Turning off the Taps: The Termination of State Sponsorship' (TPV 31:4, 733-758) - not Karlen 2017 (JPR 54:4), which the draft profile misattributed and which is about post-conflict recurrence. Integration into regular forces as the standing sticking point in proxy-conflict termination is qualitative/case-based, not estimated.

redlines.statement: Coercive attempts to dissolve, forcibly subordinate, or decapitate the organization are answered with resistance and escalation rather than submission, including against its own patron, and the response is not modulated by the cost of making it.
redlines.basis: Popovic 2017 (TPV 29:5, 922-942): sponsor coercion - detaining leaders, freezing assets - produces defection and violence against the sponsor rather than compliance, with decentralized/factionalized agents defecting most. CRS IN12186 (Wagner Group mutiny, June 2023) is the extreme observed case of an agent turning on its principal rather than submitting. This is the active face of the survival commitment above; it rests on one study's mechanism plus case evidence, which is why it is not high confidence.

redlines.statement: Will not publicly abandon the founding grievance or claim that legitimates it to its own constituency, because doing so collapses recruitment and internal cohesion; it is defended as constitutive rather than traded as a negotiating position. This is the organizational mechanism, not a claim about the sincerity of any belief.
redlines.basis: Asserted at the mechanism level in the researcher's redlines; no cited study estimates it directly. Adjacent support only: Jo 2015 (Compliant Rebels) on constituency- and recognition-facing legitimacy as the thing that moves armed-group behaviour. Weakest of the three - plausibly a strong preference rather than a genuine redline.

profiles.uncertainty:
**All three redlines carry `constraint: null`, and that is deliberate.** The engine's four constraint attributes (civilianHarmShare, legitimacyCost, visibility, attributability) describe the *character of a move* — how much harm falls on noncombatants, what it costs in legal/reputational terms, how visible it is, whether it traces back. This archetype's only non-negotiable commitments are about *the continued existence and autonomy of the organization itself*, which none of those four attributes can express. Attaching a numeric bound anyway would be inventing precision the sourcing does not supply, so the redlines are carried as prose commitments with the limitation stated here rather than dressed up as bounds.

**Explicitly no civilian-harm redline.** `counterpartHarmRestraint` is 0.30 (low confidence), and the mechanism behind it — Salehyan, Siroky & Wood 2014 (*International Organization* 68:3, 633–661) — is a *funding-structure* finding: external funding removes the need to extract resources from, and therefore court, a population. A `civilianHarmShare` bound would misrepresent that mechanism as a standing moral floor. Two corrections applied here: the paper's principal-side variable is democracy / exposure to human-rights lobbies, not autocracy (the profile's "autocratic principals restrain least" is a loose contrapositive), and the estimate is drawn from civil-war rebel organizations and is being extrapolated to contractor and cyber sub-types where it has never been tested.

**Explicitly no attribution redline.** The tempting one — "avoids provable linkage to the sponsor" — is not encoded, because the evidence splits the concept in a way the schema cannot hold. The agent often *wants* credit for its own actions (Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, documents claiming behaviour), while deniability is primarily the *sponsor's* asset (Cormac & Aldrich 2018). Clausen further finds that after October 2023 attribution ran ahead of command — actions were ascribed to a patron assessed to lack command and control. Until the engine can represent "wants own attribution, avoids sponsor attribution" as two things, this is a modeling limitation to flag, not a parameter to tune. The single value 0.35 is a midpoint between a claiming sub-type near 0.15 and a persona-based cyber front near 0.60 and describes neither.

**Two of the researcher's five redlines were dropped as preferences, not redlines.**
- *Control of the local political/territorial base and patronage economy* — its only support was "the 'control paradox' literature," which the challenge pass found has no referent anywhere in the bibliography. The citable formulations are the substitution/control trade-off (Krieg & Rickli 2019) and the principal-agent control dilemma (Byman & Kreps 2010), neither of which establishes a non-negotiable. Territorial and patronage positions do get traded; this is captured by the weights.
- *Retention of at least one external patron* — cited to the wrong Karlén paper, and empirically in tension with the redline that survives: Popovic's defecting agents accept the loss of a patron in defense of the organization. Dependence on terminable support is a strong preference, not a commitment immune to price.
- The researcher's fourth bullet (*refusal to be integrated into regular forces*) was **folded into** the survival redline rather than dropped; it is the same commitment stated as a settlement term.

**Miscitations corrected before carrying anything forward.** Karlén JPR 54:4 (2017) is about post-conflict recurrence, not sponsorship termination — the termination paper is TPV 31:4. Karlén & Rauta, "Dealers and Brokers in Civil Wars" (*International Security* 47:4, 2023) documents sponsor-side dual delegation through conduit *states*, the opposite direction from the agent-side re-delegation it was cited for. Maurer 2018's delegation/orchestration/sanctioning spectrum scores the *state's* degree of control, not the agent's preference. Moghadam & Wyss 2020 is about *nonstate sponsors* selecting proxies for political value and does not support a claiming-behaviour parameter. Mumbai 2008 was a severe but **unrealized** interstate crisis — evidence of escalation risk and sponsor loss of control, not of realized runaway escalation. RAND RR-A307-2's "geopolitical vulnerability is the primary sponsor motive" claim could not be verified and should not be leaned on.

**Least defensible parameters, ranked:** `timeHorizon` 0.45 (a midpoint between two genuine modes — defensible range 0.25–0.75); `attributionAversion` 0.35 (see above); `escalationControlBelief` 0.55 (a live scholarly disagreement — Carson 2018 versus the post-2023 analysis — that splitting the difference does not resolve; it should carry a downward trend note, and it is the one *belief* parameter on a scale of behaviours); `decisionCentralization` 0.50 (meaningless without a stated level convention: ~0.70 for a single faction, ~0.40 for a network under multiple principals; averaging two different objects is a modeling defect, not rounding); `reciprocityProportion` 0.55 (ASSUMED — no cited study estimates proportionality of agent retaliation). `ownCostTolerance` 0.62 splits two things that should not share a number: high tolerance for personnel and materiel loss, low tolerance for organization-threatening cost. `rationalityPrecision` 4 is asserted within a 3–6 band, not estimated. Confidence labels across the vector lack a published rubric and should be read as low throughout.

**Highest-leverage scenario variable:** sponsor count. Salehyan/Siroky/Wood 2014 finds that no single state can effectively restrain an organization funded by several; if the engine can represent number of principals, its effect on restraint and decision precision is larger than most differences between actor profiles.

**Presentation guardrails.** The word *archetype* must survive into any published output — printing these values as "the proxy profile" turns a modeling prior into a claim about a class of actors. And the exemplar set must not be drawn from one region or one confessional milieu: the verified sourcing already supplies non-regional cases (Karlén & Rauta 2023 on US support routed through conduit states to the Mujahideen and to UNITA; Cunningham 2010's civil-war cases; the Russian cyber-proxy ecosystem mapped in Chatham House, March 2026, Hakmeh/Moynihan/Prakash; the contractor case in CRS IN12186). Name at least two of those alongside any others used.
sources: Primary peer-reviewed (principal-agent / delegation)**

Salehyan, Idean. "The Delegation of War to Rebel Organizations." *Journal of Conflict Resolution* 54(3), 2010, 493–515. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022002709357890 — foundational P-A framing: adverse selection, moral hazard, loss of foreign-policy autonomy as the price of cost-shifting.

Salehyan, Idean; Siroky, David; Wood, Reed M. "External Rebel Sponsorship and Civilian Abuse: A Principal-Agent Analysis of Wartime Atrocities." *International Organization*, 2014. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-organization/article/abs/external-rebel-sponsorship-and-civilian-abuse-a-principalagent-analysis-of-wartime-atrocities/7B8C7423A615E804A829E95AEE9E4A39 — the single most load-bearing source for `counterpartHarmRestraint`: foreign funding reduces the need to extract resources from (and therefore court) the population, raising one-sided violence; democratic/human-rights-exposed principals restrain more; multiple principals restrain less.

Byman, Daniel & Kreps, Sarah E. "Agents of Destruction? Applying Principal-Agent Analysis to State-Sponsored Terrorism." *International Studies Perspectives* 11(1), 2010, 1–18. https://academic.oup.com/isp/article-abstract/11/1/1/1785085 — why states delegate, the control instruments they use, and where the relationship strains.

Popovic, Milos. "Fragile Proxies: Explaining Rebel Defection Against Their State Sponsors." *Terrorism and Political Violence* 29(5), 2017, 922–942. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09546553.2015.1092437 — decentralized/factionalized agents defect; coercive sponsor discipline backfires. Drives `lossFrameRiskAcceptance`, `decisionCentralization`, and the first redline. Dissertation version (open): https://www.etd.ceu.edu/2015/popovic_milos.pdf

Moghadam, Assaf & Wyss, Michel. "The Political Power of Proxies: Why Nonstate Actors Use Local Surrogates." *International Security* 44(4), 2020, 119–157. https://direct.mit.edu/isec/article-abstract/44/4/119/12248/ — proxies as political actors with their own agendas, not just military instruments; states select for military utility, nonstate sponsors for political value.

Jo, Hyeran. *Compliant Rebels: Rebel Groups and International Law in World Politics.* Cambridge UP, 2015. — legitimacy-seeking armed groups comply materially more with IHL; the reason `counterpartHarmRestraint` and `legitimacyWeight` are bimodal rather than uniformly low.

Cunningham, David E. "Blocking Resolution: How External States Can Prolong Civil Wars." *Journal of Peace Research* 47(2), 2010, 115–127. https://www.prio.org/publications/4446 — external sponsors with independent goals block termination; empirical anchor for divergent objectives.

Karlen, Niklas. "The Legacy of Foreign Patrons." *Journal of Peace Research* 54(4), 2017. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022343317700465; and "Turning off the Taps: The Termination of State Sponsorship." *Terrorism and Political Violence* 31(4). https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09546553.2017.1282861 — support is terminable; termination effects drive `timeHorizon` and the patron-retention redline.

Cormac, Rory & Aldrich, Richard J. "Grey is the new black: covert action and implausible deniability." *International Affairs* 94(3), 2018, 477–494. https://academic.oup.com/ia/article/94/3/477/4992414 — deniability is usually implausible yet still operative as *non-acknowledgement*; keeps `attributionAversion` off the ceiling.

Carson, Austin. *Secret Wars: Covert Conflict in International Politics.* Princeton UP, 2018. https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691181769/secret-wars — the case that covertness genuinely limits escalation; the strongest support for a non-trivial `escalationControlBelief`.
Doctrine-adjacent / government and think-tank**

RAND Corporation. *Proxy Warfare in Strategic Competition: Overarching Findings and Recommendations* (RR-A307-1) and *State Motivations and Future Trends* (RR-A307-2), March 2023, sponsored by the U.S. Army G-3/5/7. https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA307-1.html · https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA307-2.html — quantitative analysis of proxy wars since 1946 plus China/Iran/Russia case studies; state-supported violent nonstate actors are markedly more lethal than unsupported ones; geopolitical vulnerability is the primary sponsor motive; recommends investment in attribution as the counter-lever.

Chatham House. Hakmeh, Joyce; Moynihan, Harriet, et al. *Holding state-sponsored hackers and other cyber proxies to account*, March 2026. https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/03/holding-state-sponsored-hackers-and-other-cyber-proxies-account — maps the cyber-proxy ecosystem across intelligence units, criminal syndicates, front companies, patriotic hackers and loose hacktivists, with varying degrees of direction; deniability, sanctions insulation, and deliberately messy attribution as design features.

Maurer, Tim. *Cyber Mercenaries: The State, Hackers, and Power.* Cambridge UP, 2018 — the delegation / orchestration / sanctioning spectrum, the standard taxonomy for placing a cyber proxy on a control axis.

Krieg, Andreas & Rickli, Jean-Marc. *Surrogate Warfare: The Transformation of War in the Twenty-First Century.* Georgetown UP, 2019. https://press.georgetown.edu/Book/Surrogate-Warfare — the substitution/control trade-off stated explicitly; the conceptual spine of this profile.

Irregular Warfare Center (Mullins, Sam). *The Role of Non-State Actors as Proxies in Irregular Warfare and Malign State Influence.* https://irregularwarfarecenter.org/publications/research-studies/the-role-of-non-state-actors-as-proxies-in-irregular-warfare-and-malign-state-influence/ — U.S. government-affiliated framing of the proxy problem set.

CSIS. "Band of Brothers: The Wagner Group and the Russian State" and "Putin's Proxies: Examining Russia's Use of Private Military Companies." https://www.csis.org/blogs/post-soviet-post/band-brothers-wagner-group-and-russian-state · https://www.csis.org/analysis/putins-proxies-examining-russias-use-private-military-companies — contractor-type proxies; CRS *Wagner Group Mutiny in Russia* (IN12186) documents the June 2023 agency-slack failure in the extreme.

Clausen, Maria-Louise (DIIS). "Reassessing Principal-Agent Theory: The Houthis' evolving relationship with Iran," POMEPS, 2026. https://pomeps.org/reassessing-patron-agent-theory-the-case-of-the-houthis-evolving-relationship-to-iran — post-October-2023 evidence that attribution and control decouple: operations are ascribed to the patron even where experts assess the patron lacks command and control.
profiles.declaredVsObserved: Declared, this actor class claims legal standing, signs public humanitarian commitments, and — in concert with its patron — asserts operational independence in both directions; observed, it holds no treaty-party status and operates no legal-review apparatus, and it routinely acts outside the patron's stated preference, so the mutual independence claims are strategically produced by both sides and carry near-zero evidentiary weight in either direction. The one declaration that partly binds is the humanitarian commitment: Jo 2015 finds legitimacy-seeking organizations do change conduct measurably, but compliance tracks the organization's need for recognition and its material dependence on a local population, not the signature — model the incentive, not the declaration.

authority.statement: Go/no-go on a specific operation sits inside the armed organisation itself — a small commander circle, a military or jihad council subordinate to a governing shura, or a contractor's command staff — not with the sponsor. The sponsor supplies money, weapons, training, access and general intent through a liaison channel, and in the tightly-coupled sub-type also holds a seat or a ratification right inside the agent's governing body; what it does not reliably hold is command and control over particular operations. The archetype therefore has TWO authority nodes that must be scored separately, and the scenario must state which one a parameter refers to.
authority.basis: Byman, Daniel & Kreps, Sarah E., 'Agents of Destruction? Applying Principal-Agent Analysis to State-Sponsored Terrorism,' International Studies Perspectives 11(1), 2010, 1-18, on why states delegate and which control instruments they retain; Krieg, Andreas & Rickli, Jean-Marc, Surrogate Warfare (Georgetown UP, 2019), for the substitution/control trade-off stated explicitly. The decisive contemporary evidence for the C2 gap is Clausen, Maria-Louise (DIIS), 'Reassessing Principal-Agent Theory: The Houthis' evolving relationship with Iran,' POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, which finds the patron lacked command and control over the post-October-2023 maritime campaign while the actions were nonetheless ascribed to it. The tightly-coupled counter-case is institutionalised rather than notional: CRS In Focus IF10703, 'Lebanese Hezbollah,' updated 4 December 2024, records that Iran supplies most of the organisation's funding, training, weapons and explosives, and that the seven-member Shura Council selected a successor secretary-general in October 2024; press reporting on that council's composition and on the binding authority of the wali al-faqih (Asharq Al-Awsat, 'What We Know About Hezbollah's Shura Council,' 2024) is journalistic, not documentary, and is carried at low weight.

steps.office: Sponsor's expeditionary or external-operations directorate
steps.gate: Can withhold money, weapons, training and access, which sets the feasible option space. It does NOT approve individual operations and is routinely presented with a fait accompli. Termination of support, not veto of a plan, is the instrument this office actually holds.
steps.basis: Salehyan, Idean, 'The Delegation of War to Rebel Organizations,' Journal of Conflict Resolution 54(3), 2010, 493-515, on adverse selection and the loss of foreign-policy autonomy as the price of cost-shifting; Karlen, Niklas, 'Turning off the Taps: The Termination of State Sponsorship,' Terrorism and Political Violence 31(4), 2019, 733-758, for termination as the operative lever. The fait-accompli characterisation is supported by Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, and by the January 2024 Iraqi case in which a suspension of operations was announced two days AFTER the operation that provoked it (CNN, 30 January 2024). Authority chain as researched: an intelligence service's external branch, a defence ministry contracting office, or a state cyber command's tasking desk

steps.stage: Proposal origin — initiative inside standing intent
steps.office: Front, brigade or cell commander
steps.gate: Filters on feasibility and available means only. This stage almost never stops a proposal, because there is nothing here for it to fail: no legal adviser, no collateral-estimate cell, no interagency staffing.
steps.basis: The absence is the finding, and it is an inference from institutional structure rather than a measured fact — no cited study inventories legal-review bodies across proxy organisations. The supporting evidence is that armed groups hold no treaty-party status and build compliance machinery only when pursuing recognition (Jo, Hyeran, Compliant Rebels: Rebel Groups and International Law in World Politics, Cambridge UP, 2015), and that the concealed sub-type is structured as commercial employment rather than command (U.S. Department of Justice, 'Seven Iranians Working for Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Affiliated Entities Charged...', 24 March 2016, describing defendants employed by ITSecTeam and Mersad Company, firms performing work on behalf of the Iranian government including the IRGC). Flagged low: an absence is the hardest thing in this dossier to source positively. Authority chain as researched: in the concealed sub-type, a contracted front company or a persona-operating team under a state cyber unit

steps.office: The armed organisation's military council or commander circle
steps.gate: Approves or refuses on three tests: expected effect on the organisation's own constituency, expected effect on the patron relationship, and organisational survivability. Legal exposure and harm to the counterpart's noncombatants are not tests at this gate, which is the structural reason counterpartHarmRestraint sits low in the profile rather than a claim about anyone's character.
steps.basis: The constituency test and its conditionality are from Jo 2015 (legitimacy-seeking, territory-governing groups comply materially more) and Salehyan, Idean; Siroky, David; Wood, Reed M., 'External Rebel Sponsorship and Civilian Abuse: A Principal-Agent Analysis of Wartime Atrocities,' International Organization 68(3), 2014, 633-661 — externally funded groups do not need to extract from, and therefore do not need to court, the population. The survivability test is from Popovic, Milos, 'Fragile Proxies: Explaining Rebel Defection Against Their State Sponsors,' Terrorism and Political Violence 29(5), 2017, 922-942. Note the out-of-sample risk the profile already flags: the 2014 estimate is drawn from civil-war rebel organisations and is being extended to contractor and cyber sub-types where it has never been tested. Authority chain as researched: a jihad/military council reporting to a governing shura, a militia's leadership office, or a contractor's command staff

steps.stage: Patron consultation or ratification — institutionalised in the tightly-coupled sub-type, absent in the loosely-coupled one
steps.office: Resident patron liaison element
steps.gate: Can delay or veto where the relationship institutionalises it. Where it does not, it is bypassed, informed in parallel, or told afterwards. The failure of this gate is the archetype's characteristic failure mode and the single most consequential source of variance in its behaviour.
steps.basis: Byman & Kreps 2010 on the control dilemma; Popovic 2017 on decentralised and factionalised agents defecting most. The clearest documented failure is Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, finding the patron lacked command and control over a campaign that escalated counter to its preferences. The clearest documented success of a POLITICAL rather than patron gate is the Iraqi case of 30 January 2024, where the stated reason for suspending operations was avoiding embarrassment to the host government (Al Jazeera, 'Kataib Hezbollah announces halt of attacks on US forces,' 31 January 2024) — and even there the gate operated after execution, not before it. Authority chain as researched: or a patron seat / ratification right inside the agent's governing council

steps.office: The organisation's military media office (claiming sub-type) or the persona/front handler (concealed sub-type)
steps.gate: Decides whether the act is claimed openly, claimed under a persona, or left unclaimed. This is the one stage that consistently and deliberately shapes political effect, and it can reverse the sign of attributionAversion: the same archetype that hides its operators will broadcast the operation.
steps.basis: Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, documents open claiming and the deliberate internationalisation of a campaign; the joint advisory of CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA, Israel INCD, Canada CCCS and UK NCSC, AA23-335A, 'IRGC-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit PLCs in Multiple Sectors, Including U.S. Water and Wastewater Systems Facilities,' first published 1 December 2023 and later updated, records a persona defacement banner claiming targets while the operators stayed concealed. Cormac, Rory & Aldrich, Richard J., 'Grey is the new black: covert action and implausible deniability,' International Affairs 94(3), 2018, 477-494, establishes that non-acknowledgement is the SPONSOR's asset — the two nodes want different things at this gate, which is why the profile's single 0.35 describes neither.

steps.office: Executing cell or unit
steps.gate: Stops nothing. The sponsor's only remaining instrument is denial, and denial is a sponsor-side move that changes the agent's conduct not at all — modelling it as a brake on the agent is a level-of-analysis error.
steps.basis: Cormac & Aldrich 2018 on non-acknowledgement operating even where deniability is implausible. The observed case is the 7-8 February 2018 engagement near Khasham, Deir ez-Zor, where a force including Russian private military contractors was destroyed by U.S. air and artillery strikes and the Russian government never acknowledged participation in the ground operation (Middle East Institute, 'Syria is where the conflict between Wagner and the Russian government began'; CSIS, 'Band of Brothers: The Wagner Group and the Russian State'). Authority chain as researched: separately, the sponsor's public-affairs and diplomatic apparatus

tempo.statement: Short and highly variable: hours to days from proposal to execution for a prepared option, because the path carries no legal review, no interagency staffing and no legislative notification. What compresses it is the size of the go/no-go circle; what stalls it is materiel resupply through the patron's channel and, in the tightly-coupled sub-type only, waiting on a ratification the loosely-coupled sub-type does not wait on. The corollary matters more than the number: the brake, when it appears, appears AFTER execution as a public announcement rather than before it as a gate.
tempo.basis: ASSUMED, not measured — no located study times the decision cycle of proxy organisations, and this is an inference from the step structure above. The post-hoc-brake observation is the sourced part: the Iraqi suspension announcement of 30 January 2024 followed the 28 January Tower 22 strike by two days (CNN, 30 January 2024; Al Jazeera, 31 January 2024), and the Houthi narrowing of 19-20 January 2025 followed fourteen months of campaign (Raydan, Noam & Nadimi, Farzin, 'Despite the Houthi Pledge to Limit Attacks, the Red Sea Remains Highly Volatile,' The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 27 January 2025). Popovic 2017 supports independent action by decentralised agents but estimates no timing.

preconditions.statement: A patron relationship supplying money, weapons, training or access that the organisation does not have to raise from the population it operates among. This is the archetype's definitional condition and the mechanism behind most of its other parameters.
preconditions.basis: Salehyan, Siroky & Wood, International Organization 68(3), 2014, 633-661 — external funding removes the need to extract resources from, and therefore to court, a local population, which is the estimated pathway to higher one-sided violence. Salehyan, Journal of Conflict Resolution 54(3), 2010, supplies the principal-side logic. This is the best-estimated claim in the dossier; the qualifier is that it is estimated on civil-war rebel organisations.

preconditions.statement: A grievance or constituency claim the operation can be publicly attached to. The organisation is reluctant to act where it cannot narrate the act to its own base, which is why campaigns are declared as linkage to a larger cause rather than as local opportunism.
preconditions.basis: Jo 2015 on constituency- and recognition-facing legitimacy as the thing that moves armed-group behaviour; Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, on the deliberate declaration of a Gaza linkage and the internationalisation it bought. ASSERTED at mechanism level — no study estimates a narratability precondition, and the counter-example class (unclaimed operations by concealed sub-types) is real, which is why this is low rather than medium.

preconditions.statement: Survivable organisational exposure. The operation must not put the organisation's existence, its command, or its armed autonomy at risk — a far tighter constraint than loss of personnel or materiel, which the archetype absorbs readily.
preconditions.basis: Popovic 2017 (TPV 29:5, 922-942): coercive discipline aimed at the organisation itself produces defection rather than compliance, so organisational risk and personnel risk are priced differently. This is the precondition that generates the profile's first redline and the gap between its ownCostTolerance value (0.62) and the higher figure a casualty-only reading would give.

preconditions.statement: For the concealed sub-type, a usable cover layer standing BEFORE the operation, not improvised after it: a front company, a contracted team, or a claimed persona with its own presence.
preconditions.basis: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 'Seven Iranians Working for Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Affiliated Entities Charged for Conducting Coordinated Campaign of Cyber Attacks Against U.S. Financial Sector,' 24 March 2016 (SDNY indictment returned 21 January 2016), describing two Iran-based computer companies performing work on behalf of the Iranian government including the IRGC; Maurer, Tim, Cyber Mercenaries: The State, Hackers, and Power (Cambridge UP, 2018) for the delegation/orchestration/sanctioning taxonomy; Chatham House (Hakmeh, Joyce; Moynihan, Harriet, et al.), 'Holding state-sponsored hackers and other cyber proxies to account,' research paper published 25 March 2026 (ISBN 978 1 78413 677 2), on front companies and deliberately messy attribution as design features. NOTE ON SCOPE: that paper's empirical base is Russia's cyber-proxy ecosystem, so its use here is an archetype-level extension beyond the case it studies.

afterAction.statement: Weak, and public rather than institutional. No standing lessons-learned body appears anywhere in the open record for any sub-type. What is observable instead is post-hoc leadership statements conceding miscalibration and adjusting the boundaries of the next campaign — and the adjustment is visible in conduct for the centralised, territorially-governing sub-type while the decentralised sub-types show no such trace at all. Treat learning in this archetype as leadership-circle memory, not institutional process, which also means it is destroyed by decapitation in a way a state's after-action process is not.
afterAction.basis: The strongest single instance is the organisation's own secretary-general stating publicly, in an Al-Jadeed television interview on 27 August 2006, that the 12 July cross-border raid would not have been ordered had the resulting war been foreseen and that such a response had been considered inconceivable (Haaretz, 'Nasrallah: We Wouldn't Have Snatched Soldiers if We Thought It Would Spark War,' 27-28 August 2006; Al Jazeera, 'Nasrallah says he did not want war,' 27 August 2006; MEMRI TV archival clip of the same interview - MEMRI is an advocacy translation organisation reporting on an adversary and is carried here only as a second locator for a broadcast the two press accounts independently report). CAVEATS, both material: the statement is self-serving (it doubles as a claim of non-culpability for the war), and one leadership statement is thin evidence for an institutional property. No study of after-action process in proxy organisations was located.

declaredEnds.statement: Ending an occupation or an external military presence, stated as the organisation's founding purpose and as the condition on which its own continued existence rests. The declaration is load-bearing: it is what makes disarmament unofferable rather than merely expensive.
declaredEnds.basis: Stated in organisation-issued documents across the governing/insurgent sub-type — Hezbollah's 1985 Open Letter and its 2009 Political Document both frame resistance to occupation and foreign tutelage as constitutive — and repeated in operational statements, e.g. the 30 January 2024 Iraqi announcement framing operations as against 'the occupation forces' (CNN, 30 January 2024; Al Jazeera, 31 January 2024). ARCHETYPE-LEVEL CAUTION: this is the modal declared end across governing and insurgent sub-types, not a universal — contractor sub-types declare a commercial and state-service purpose instead, and cyber front organisations declare nothing at all beyond a persona's banner text.

declaredEnds.statement: Linkage — acting in declared support of an allied campaign elsewhere, and saying so, so that the operation reads to its own base and to third parties as solidarity rather than local opportunism. The declared linkage doubles as a declared termination condition, which is one of the few places this archetype publishes something falsifiable about its own stopping rule.
declaredEnds.basis: Clausen, Maria-Louise (DIIS), 'Reassessing Principal-Agent Theory: The Houthis' evolving relationship with Iran,' POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, on the declared Gaza linkage and its deliberate internationalisation. The falsifiable part was tested and largely held: after the Gaza ceasefire the movement notified shipping on 19-20 January 2025 that attacks would be limited to Israeli-flagged or wholly Israeli-owned vessels (Al Jazeera, 'Yemen's Houthis to only target Israel-linked ships following Gaza ceasefire,' 20 January 2025) and released the Galaxy Leader's crew on 22 January 2025 (Raydan & Nadimi, The Washington Institute, 27 January 2025) — the same analysis cautions that the pledge left U.S. and U.K. shipping explicitly exposed.

declaredEnds.statement: Recognition and legal standing for the organisation as a legitimate armed formation — pursued through the host state's own law where that route exists, and pursued in a form that confers status and salary without dissolving the organisation's separate chain of command.
declaredEnds.basis: Iraq's Law No. 40 of 2016 (Law of the Popular Mobilization Authority), enacted 26 November 2016, recognised the Popular Mobilization Commission as part of the state's armed forces under the commander-in-chief while constituent formations retained their own commands (contemporary reporting: RFE/RL, 26 November 2016; analysis: The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 'Iraq's PMF Law Is No Substitute for Real Security Reform'; RAND Corporation, RR-A722-1, 'The Future of the Iraqi Popular Mobilization Forces: Lessons from Historical Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration Efforts'). Jo 2015 supplies the general mechanism by which recognition-seeking changes conduct. The law's text and later amendments are contested in translation; the behavioural outcome — legal status taken, command retained — is not.

selfImage.statement: A resistance or defence organisation with an independent mandate, not an instrument: the self-description is 'we decide, the patron supports.' The claim is asserted in both directions because it serves both parties — the patron's denial and the agent's autonomy claim are the same product. The contractor sub-type inverts the surface (a private commercial firm performing lawful services) while making the identical functional claim of separation from the state.
selfImage.basis: The profile's own declaredVsObserved section already establishes that the mutual independence claims are strategically produced by both sides and carry near-zero evidentiary weight in either direction; Cormac & Aldrich 2018 explains why the sponsor half is produced. The one piece of evidence that the agent's half is not purely theatre is behavioural, not declaratory: Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, documents the agent escalating counter to the patron's preferences. DELIBERATE OMISSION, recorded here because an absent field is otherwise invisible to a reader: `declaredIdeology` is left unset. This profile is an archetype prior over a family of organisations, and no charter, programme or strategic concept was ever issued by 'the state-aligned proxy' — writing one would mean generalising a single exemplar's founding document to a class, which is the exact inference the schema's structural refusal exists to block. Sub-type exemplars do issue such documents (the 1985 Open Letter and 2009 Political Document above are examples), and they belong at the scenario level when a specific organisation is instantiated, not here.

threatModel.statement: Disarmament, dissolution, or absorption into a state's regular forces — named as existential and treated as existential regardless of which direction it comes from, including from its own patron.
threatModel.basis: Popovic 2017 (TPV 29:5, 922-942) supplies the mechanism: coercive sponsor discipline produces defection rather than compliance. The observed case is documentary and dated: the Russian Ministry of Defence's order of 10 June 2023 requiring all volunteer formations to sign contracts with it by 1 July, the contractor's public refusal on 11 June (RFE/RL, 'Wagner Chief Refuses To Obey Decree In Latest Spat With Russian Defense Minister,' 11 June 2023; CNN, 11 June 2023), and the armed mutiny that followed on 23-24 June (Congressional Research Service, Insight IN12186, 'Wagner Group Mutiny in Russia,' 28 June 2023). This is the best-evidenced item in the dossier.

threatModel.statement: Termination or diversion of patron support — the instrument the patron actually holds, and the archetype's principal material vulnerability. Note that this is a vulnerability the archetype will nonetheless accept rather than submit, which is why it is a threat and not a redline.
threatModel.basis: Karlen, Niklas, 'Turning off the Taps: The Termination of State Sponsorship,' Terrorism and Political Violence 31(4), 2019, 733-758. The 'accepts it rather than submits' qualifier comes from Popovic 2017's defecting agents and from the June 2023 contractor case above, and is the reason the profile's uncertainty section dropped patron-retention from the redline list.

threatModel.statement: Decapitation of the leadership circle and the intelligence penetration that enables it. Because go/no-go authority is concentrated in a small circle and after-action learning is that circle's memory, decapitation costs this archetype disproportionately more than it costs a state.
threatModel.basis: Inferred from response rather than from declaration — no located source states this threat in the archetype's own terms. The observable trace is that CRS In Focus IF10703, 'Lebanese Hezbollah,' updated 4 December 2024, records the Shura Council selecting a successor secretary-general in October 2024 following the incumbent's death, i.e. the succession machinery existed and functioned, which cuts against the strongest version of this claim. Carried at low confidence and flagged as the weakest item in this section.

threatModel.statement: Attribution that is credible enough to move the patron — not attribution as such. The archetype fears the consequence of linkage (support withdrawn, patron sanctioned into retreat) rather than exposure, which is why it will claim its own operations while resisting proof of sponsorship.
threatModel.basis: Cormac & Aldrich 2018 on non-acknowledgement surviving implausible deniability; RAND Corporation, RR-A307-1, Proxy Warfare in Strategic Competition: Overarching Findings and Recommendations (March 2023, sponsored by U.S. Army G-3/5/7), which recommends investment in attribution precisely as the counter-lever. The complication is documented: Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, finds that after October 2023 attribution ran ahead of command — actions were ascribed to a patron assessed to lack command and control — so attribution is decoupling from the thing it is supposed to prove.

adversaryModel.statement: Expects the adversary to respond, and to respond disproportionately, but to stop short of moves that would end the organisation — a belief that has been repeatedly wrong at the top of the ladder and repeatedly confirmed below it. Sub-threshold action is read as tolerated because it has in fact been tolerated, and the belief updates only after an unexpectedly large response. The archetype also expects the adversary to be constrained by third parties — host-government politics, allied opinion, escalation-aversion — in ways it does not believe itself to be constrained.
adversaryModel.basis: INFERRED FROM BEHAVIOUR, not from any declared assessment; no located source states this archetype's adversary model in its own words, which is why this is low confidence. The two anchors are the 2006 admission that a war-scale response had been considered inconceivable (Haaretz and Al Jazeera, 27-28 August 2006, reporting the 27 August Al-Jadeed interview) and the post-October-2023 pattern in which the speed and degree of attribution and response outran the actors' expectations (Clausen, POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026). Carson, Austin, Secret Wars: Covert Conflict in International Politics (Princeton UP, 2018) is the strongest support for covertness genuinely limiting escalation, but it is a STATE-level finding and importing it to the agent node repeats the level-of-analysis error the profile's escalationControlBelief basis warns about; it is cited here as adjacent, not as support.

history.episode: A Lebanese armed organisation conducted a cross-border raid that killed three and captured two Israeli soldiers, triggering a 34-day war. Six weeks later the organisation's secretary-general stated on Lebanese television that the raid would not have been ordered had the resulting war been foreseen, and that a response on that scale had been considered inconceivable.
history.choice: Acted at a rung it judged to be tit-for-tat, absorbed the resulting war rather than capitulating, and then publicly conceded the escalation estimate had been wrong.
history.lesson: Acted, then absorbed. The organisation believed it controlled the rung it was stepping onto and did not; it did not fold when the response came. This is the archetype's clearest single case of high escalation-control BELIEF paired with poor escalation-control CALIBRATION — the distinction the profile deliberately preserves by keeping escalationControlBelief a belief parameter rather than a behaviour.
history.basis: Contemporaneous reporting of the 27 August 2006 Al-Jadeed interview: Haaretz, 'Nasrallah: We Wouldn't Have Snatched Soldiers if We Thought It Would Spark War,' 27-28 August 2006; Al Jazeera, 'Nasrallah says he did not want war,' 27 August 2006; MEMRI TV archival clip of the same broadcast, carried as a locator only and read as an interested source. Two caveats: the admission is self-serving, doubling as a disclaimer of responsibility for the war, and a leadership statement is evidence about a declared estimate, not about the internal process that produced it.

history.episode: A contractor employed by one of two Iran-based computer companies performing work on behalf of the Iranian government, including the IRGC, obtained unauthorised access to the SCADA systems of the Bowman Avenue Dam in Rye Brook, New York, in August and September 2013. The conduct was charged in a Southern District of New York indictment returned 21 January 2016 and unsealed 24 March 2016, alongside a DDoS campaign against 46 U.S. financial-sector and other targets running from late 2011 to mid-2013.
history.choice: Acted through commercial cover rather than organically, and stopped at access.
history.lesson: Acted through a delegated corporate layer — the concealed sub-type's default, and the strongest documentary instance of it, because the employment relationship is stated in a charging document rather than inferred from tradecraft. This episode is deliberately NOT offered as evidence about counterpartHarmRestraint: contemporaneous reporting indicates the dam's sluice gate had been manually disconnected for maintenance during the intrusion, so restraint and incapacity are observationally identical here and scoring it either way would be inventing a finding.
history.basis: U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 'Seven Iranians Working for Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Affiliated Entities Charged for Conducting Coordinated Campaign of Cyber Attacks Against U.S. Financial Sector,' 24 March 2016; FBI Cyber Most Wanted, 'Iranian DDoS Attacks.' The DOJ page returned HTTP 403 to direct retrieval during this research pass, so the sluice-gate detail is carried from contemporaneous reporting of the department's statement (Help Net Security, 24 March 2016) and was NOT verified against the primary text in this review — treat that specific detail as unverified.

history.episode: Iraq's parliament enacted Law No. 40 of 2016, the Law of the Popular Mobilization Authority, recognising the Popular Mobilization Commission as part of the state's armed forces under the commander-in-chief. Constituent armed formations took the legal status, the payroll and the state cover; they retained their own chains of command, and successive integration and dissolution initiatives in the years since have not produced disarmament.
history.choice: Accepted state legal cover; declined dissolution of its own command.
history.lesson: Held the line that mattered and took everything else. The archetype's legitimacy behaviour in its purest observable form: legitimacy is instrumented, not internalised, and the parts of it that cost armed autonomy are refused at any price. This is the cleanest behavioural backing for the profile's survival redline, because the offer on the table — legal standing plus a state salary — was substantial and moved the commitment not at all.
history.basis: Law No. 40 of 2016 as enacted 26 November 2016 (contemporary reporting: RFE/RL, 26 November 2016); The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 'Iraq's PMF Law Is No Substitute for Real Security Reform'; RAND Corporation, RR-A722-1, 'The Future of the Iraqi Popular Mobilization Forces: Lessons from Historical Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration Efforts.' The law's text and its later amendments are contested in translation and in what they actually require of constituent formations; the behavioural outcome is not contested.

history.episode: A pro-regime force including Russian private military contractors advanced on a U.S.-partnered position near the Conoco gas facility at Khasham, east of the Euphrates in Deir ez-Zor province, and was destroyed by U.S. air and artillery strikes over 7-8 February 2018. The Russian government has never acknowledged participation in the ground operation.
history.choice: Acted, absorbed heavy loss, and was publicly disowned by its sponsor.
history.lesson: Acted and absorbed. Personnel loss on a scale a state force would treat as a strategic defeat did not end the organisation's operations or its relationship with the sponsor — this is the case behind the high half of the profile's bimodal ownCostTolerance, and it sits alongside the June 2023 case that shows the low half (costs threatening the organisation itself). The denial that followed was the sponsor's move, not the agent's, and changed nothing about the agent's conduct.
history.basis: Middle East Institute, 'Syria is where the conflict between Wagner and the Russian government began'; CSIS, 'Band of Brothers: The Wagner Group and the Russian State' and 'Putin's Proxies: Examining Russia's Use of Private Military Companies.' CONTESTED NUMBER, and the contest is itself informative: open estimates of contractor dead range from roughly a dozen to over two hundred, with no authoritative count, because neither the sponsor nor the organisation published one. Do not carry any specific casualty figure from this episode into a parameter.

history.episode: After the Russian Ministry of Defence ordered all volunteer formations to sign contracts with it by 1 July (order of 10 June 2023) and the contractor force publicly refused on 11 June, the organisation on 23-24 June seized the Southern Military District headquarters at Rostov-on-Don and advanced a column toward Moscow, standing down that evening under a negotiated arrangement.
history.choice: Refused subordination, escalated against its own principal, then held short of the capital once survival terms were on offer.
history.lesson: Refused, escalated, held — the sequence Popovic's mechanism predicts, run to its extreme. Coercive formalisation by the patron produced armed defection rather than compliance, which is why the profile treats raising the price of subordination as moving the commitment the wrong way. The halt is the load-bearing half: the escalation stopped the moment organisational survival was addressed, which shows it was instrumental to survival rather than to any wider objective, and shows the archetype will stop when the thing it was defending is secured.
history.basis: Congressional Research Service, Insight IN12186, 'Wagner Group Mutiny in Russia,' 28 June 2023; RFE/RL, 'Wagner Chief Refuses To Obey Decree In Latest Spat With Russian Defense Minister,' 11 June 2023; CNN, 'Wagner chief says he won't sign contracts with Russia's Defense Ministry,' 11 June 2023. Mechanism: Popovic, Milos, 'Fragile Proxies,' Terrorism and Political Violence 29(5), 2017, 922-942. The sequence of events is well documented; the terms of the stand-down and who brokered them remain opaque, so the reasoning attributed to the halt is inference.

history.episode: A Yemeni armed movement seized the vehicle carrier Galaxy Leader in the southern Red Sea on 19 November 2023 and opened a publicly claimed, branded maritime campaign, announced operation by operation through its own military spokesman and declared as conditional on the war in Gaza. After the January 2025 Gaza ceasefire, its Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center notified shipping on 19-20 January 2025 that attacks would be limited to Israeli-flagged or wholly Israeli-owned vessels, and the twenty-five-member Galaxy Leader crew was released on 22 January 2025.
history.choice: Acted and claimed, against its patron's assessed preference; later narrowed the target set and released the crew when the condition it had itself declared was met.
history.lesson: Acted, claimed, then held to its own published terms. The concealed-proxy intuition inverts here: the organisation wanted the credit, because claiming is what converts a local movement into a regional actor and demonstrates value to a patron. The narrowing matters more than the campaign for modelling purposes — it is the rare case where this archetype published a stopping rule and then followed it, which is why reciprocityProportion should not be read as uniformly disproportionate.
history.basis: Clausen, Maria-Louise (DIIS), 'Reassessing Principal-Agent Theory: The Houthis' evolving relationship with Iran,' POMEPS Studies 58, March 2026, which finds the patron lacked command and control over the campaign while the actions were ascribed to it; Al Jazeera, 'Yemen's Houthis to only target Israel-linked ships following Gaza ceasefire,' 20 January 2025; Raydan, Noam & Nadimi, Farzin, 'Despite the Houthi Pledge to Limit Attacks, the Red Sea Remains Highly Volatile,' The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 27 January 2025, which records the 22 January crew release and cautions that the pledge left U.S. and U.K. shipping explicitly exposed and that targeting had repeatedly rested on inaccurate vessel-ownership information; CRS In Focus IF12581, 'Yemen: Conflict, Red Sea Security, and U.S. Policy,' for chronology. The 'followed its own rule' reading is contested by the same Washington Institute analysis and should be carried as a qualified finding.

history.episode: A persona-operating team affiliated with Iran's IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command compromised internet-exposed Unitronics Vision-series PLC/HMI devices by authenticating over default credentials on TCP port 20256 — at least 75 devices, including at least 34 in the U.S. water and wastewater sector, among them the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa, Pennsylvania on 25 November 2023 — and left a defacement banner claiming the devices as targets because they were Israeli-made.
history.choice: Acted at defacement grade against a lifeline service, claimed the act loudly under a persona, and kept its operators and its state unit concealed.
history.lesson: Acted and claimed while hiding — the two halves of attribution that the profile's single 0.35 cannot hold at once. The persona claimed immediately; the state unit behind it was named roughly two months later by sanctions, not by the claim. Whether stopping short of manipulating process control was restraint or simply the ceiling of a default-credential operation is not established, so this episode is deliberately not offered as evidence about counterpartHarmRestraint.
history.basis: Joint cybersecurity advisory of CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA, Israel's National Cyber Directorate, Canada's CCCS and the UK NCSC, AA23-335A, 'IRGC-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit PLCs in Multiple Sectors, Including U.S. Water and Wastewater Systems Facilities,' first published 1 December 2023 and subsequently updated, for device counts, access method and banner text; U.S. Department of the Treasury press release JY2072, 'Treasury Sanctions Actors Responsible for Malicious Cyber Activities on Critical Infrastructure,' 2 February 2024, designating six officials of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command for directing the activity. Facts of the operation are high-confidence government reporting; the inference about intent is not.

history.episode: Two days after a one-way drone strike on the Tower 22 logistics outpost in northeast Jordan killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded dozens on 28 January 2024, an Iran-backed Iraqi armed group announced the suspension of its military operations against U.S. forces, giving as the reason the avoidance of embarrassment to the Iraqi government, instructing its fighters to adopt 'passive defence' temporarily, and stating it would continue to support Gaza by other means.
history.choice: Held — announced a unilateral suspension after an operation whose consequences it had not sought.
history.lesson: Held, and held for a host-government political reason rather than a military one. This is the clearest documented pull-back in the set, and it locates the brake precisely: not in a pre-execution gate but in a post-hoc announcement two days after the effect, which is exactly what a decision path with no legal or interagency review predicts. It also shows the archetype's legitimacy weight is real but narrow — the constituency and host-government relationship bind where international law does not.
history.basis: CNN, 'Kataib Hezbollah: Powerful Iran-backed militia in Iraq to suspend military ops against US forces in region,' 30 January 2024; Al Jazeera, 'Kataib Hezbollah announces halt of attacks on US forces,' 31 January 2024; The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 'Kataib Hezbollah Secretary-General Tries to Forestall U.S. Strikes,' 2024. TWO LIMITS ON THIS EVIDENCE: attribution of the Tower 22 strike to this specific group is a U.S. assessment and was not claimed in those terms by the group, and attacks on U.S. positions resumed within months — this is a tactical hold, not a durable restraint, and should not be scored as one.

history.episode: From 8 October 2023 an armed organisation on Israel's northern border opened a deliberately bounded attrition campaign — anti-tank fire, drones and short-range rockets held to a narrow band along the Blue Line — declining for roughly eleven months to open the general war its declared arsenal allowed, before the front expanded sharply in September 2024 and the organisation's senior leadership was killed.
history.choice: Held at a self-imposed geographic and target ceiling for eleven months, then absorbed a decapitating campaign rather than capitulating.
history.lesson: Held, then absorbed. The longest-running restraint case in the set, and the reason reciprocityProportion sits near the middle rather than high: when both organisational survival and domestic standing are at stake, this archetype calibrates rather than answers in kind, and it deliberately underuses capability it has publicly claimed. The ceiling was its own and it did not hold — the same organisation then chose absorption over terms.
history.basis: Byman, Daniel; Jones, Seth G.; Palmer, Alexander, 'Escalating to War between Israel, Hezbollah, and Iran,' Center for Strategic and International Studies, Warfare, Irregular Threats, and Terrorism Program, 4 October 2024: between 7 October 2023 and 31 August 2024 the average Israeli strike fell about 4 km into Lebanon and the average Hezbollah strike about 3 km into Israel, while during the week of 22 September 2024 those averages were 27 km and 28 km respectively; the same analysis records that the organisation 'kept its rocket attacks small relative to its total launch capacity' against a claimed inventory of as many as 200,000 standoff weapons, and attributes the earlier limits to a combination of Hezbollah restraint and Israeli deterrence. The Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 'Hezbollah's Escalation Ladder,' for the rung structure.
